**Stanley Alan Van Gundy** (born August 26, 1959)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-bbr-1) is an American former [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") coach who is a television commentator for _[College Basketball on CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College\_Basketball\_on\_CBS "College Basketball on CBS")_ for [CBS Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Sports "CBS Sports") and _[NBA on Prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA\_on\_Prime "NBA on Prime")_ for [Sports on Amazon Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_on_Amazon_Prime_Video "Sports on Amazon Prime Video"). He previously worked as game analyst for [NBA on TNT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_TNT "NBA on TNT") from [2019 to 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_NBA_season "2019–20 NBA season"), and again from [2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_NBA_season "2021–22 NBA season") to [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024%E2%80%9325_NBA_season "2024–25 NBA season"). Prior to TNT, he was most recently the head coach for the [New Orleans Pelicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_Pelicans "New Orleans Pelicans") of the NBA. He also served as the head coach and president of basketball operations for the [Detroit Pistons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Pistons "Detroit Pistons") from 2014 to 2018.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-vangundy-2) From 2003 to 2005, he was the head coach of the [Miami Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Heat "Miami Heat") but resigned in 2005 mid-season, returning the job over to [Pat Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Riley "Pat Riley"). Van Gundy then coached the Orlando Magic for five seasons from 2007 to 2012, leading them to the [2009 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_Finals "2009 NBA Finals"). He is the older brother of former [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks") and [Houston Rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Rockets "Houston Rockets") head coach [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy").

## Playing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Playing career")]

Van Gundy was a starting guard at [Alhambra High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra_High_School_(Martinez,_California) "Alhambra High School (Martinez, California)") in [Martinez, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martinez,_California "Martinez, California") in the [San Francisco Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area"). After his senior year, he played for an all-county team that also included [Kenny Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Carter "Ken Carter"), whose coaching career was the basis for _[Coach Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coach\_Carter "Coach Carter")_, a Hollywood feature film starring [Samuel L. Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_L._Jackson "Samuel L. Jackson"). Van Gundy played college basketball for his father, [Bill Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Van_Gundy "Bill Van Gundy"), at [SUNY-Brockport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York_at_Brockport "State University of New York at Brockport"), a Division III school, until he graduated in 1981 with a B.A. in English and a B.S. in Physical Education.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-heatbio-3)

## Coaching career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Coaching career")]

### College

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: College")]

Van Gundy began his coaching career as an assistant coach at the [University of Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Vermont "University of Vermont"), 1981–83, and was head coach at [Castleton State College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castleton_State_College "Castleton State College") in Vermont for three seasons from 1983 to 1986.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-heatbio-3) After his first season as Castleton head coach, the NAIA named Van Gundy the District 5 Coach of the Year.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-Wisconsin_top_assistant-4) Castleton finished 1984–85 the top team in the [NAIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Intercollegiate_Athletics "National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics")'s Mayflower Conference and won the NAIA District 5 tournament.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-6) After serving as an assistant coach at [Canisius College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canisius_College "Canisius College") in 1987 and [Fordham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fordham_University "Fordham University") in 1988, Van Gundy was named head coach at the University of Lowell. During his four-season tenure at the school, which saw the institution become the [University of Massachusetts Lowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Massachusetts_Lowell "University of Massachusetts Lowell"), he compiled a record of 54–60 and coached Leo Parent, whom Van Gundy called "the best Division 2 player in the nation."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-7)

Van Gundy then became an assistant at the [University of Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Madison "University of Wisconsin–Madison") under [Stu Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stu_Jackson "Stu Jackson").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-heatbio-3) When Jackson left after 2 years to become general manager of the expansion NBA Vancouver franchise, Van Gundy was promoted to replace him as head coach and given a 5-year contract. Coming off an 18–11 season with future NBA star [Michael Finley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Finley "Michael Finley") back for his senior year and highly touted recruits coming in, the team went into the season with high expectations, but ended with a disappointing 13–14 record (7–11 and ninth place in the Big 10). Van Gundy was fired at the end of the season and given a buyout for the 4 years remaining on his contract. Van Gundy blamed financial concerns at the school for his firing.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-8) The team would go on to hire [Dick Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Bennett "Dick Bennett") from the [University of Wisconsin–Green Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Green_Bay "University of Wisconsin–Green Bay") and he finished his first year with a 17–15 record and NIT appearance despite losing Finley and other key players.

Overall, Van Gundy compiled a record of 135–92 (.595) in eight years as a college head coach.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-heatbio-3)

### Miami Heat

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Miami Heat")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/StanVanGundy_20050723_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-StanVanGundy_20050723_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:StanVanGundy_20050723_(cropped).jpg)

Van Gundy in 2005

When [Pat Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Riley "Pat Riley") left the [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks") to coach the [Miami Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Heat "Miami Heat"), the Knicks refused to let him hire [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy"), perhaps his most valuable assistant. Riley hired Stan, his brother, saying "I wanted at least one Van Gundy with me".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-berkow19970420-9) Stan Van Gundy spent 12 years with the Heat. After working as an assistant under Riley, Van Gundy was named head coach when Riley abruptly resigned as coach prior to the [2003–04 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003%E2%80%9304_NBA_season "2003–04 NBA season"). However, Riley remained as President of the team. Van Gundy took over a team that had won 25 games the previous season. He led them to a 42-win season, in which they won a very high percentage of their late season games and surprised many by advancing to the second round of the [2004 NBA playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_NBA_playoffs "2004 NBA playoffs"), nearly defeating the team with the league's best record, the [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Pacers "Indiana Pacers"), with Van Gundy's dynamic coaching showcasing the strong play of rookie [Dwyane Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwyane_Wade "Dwyane Wade").

During the off-season, [Shaquille O'Neal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaquille_O'Neal "Shaquille O'Neal") demanded a trade and made Miami the only viable option for the Lakers to make a transaction with. Riley gave up [Caron Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caron_Butler "Caron Butler"), [Lamar Odom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamar_Odom "Lamar Odom"), [Brian Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Grant "Brian Grant") and a future first-round [draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_draft "NBA draft") choice, replacing three of the team's starters, including an Olympian, with O'Neal. Van Gundy led the Heat to the best record in the [Eastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Conference_(NBA) "Eastern Conference (NBA)") in the first half of the season, becoming the first Heat coach to coach in the [All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_NBA_All-Star_Game "2005 NBA All-Star Game"), where he led the East to a victory. The Heat finished the season with 59 wins, earning the best record in the conference. The Heat went on to advance to Game 7 of the Eastern Conference finals, where they lost to the [Detroit Pistons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Pistons "Detroit Pistons"). Injuries played a factor in their defeat, particularly a rib injury to leading scorer Wade during Game 5, which prevented him from playing Game 6 and severely hindered him in Game 7, both Piston wins.

During the 2005 off-season, it was widely speculated that Pat Riley was attempting to run Van Gundy out of his coaching job and take over the job himself, now that the team was in a position to contend for the championship.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-go-10) Van Gundy would resign from his position as head coach on December 12, 2005, just 21 games into the season, citing a need to spend more time with his family. Riley replaced him as head coach, and led Miami to their first championship that same season.

In [Shaquille O'Neal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaquille_O'Neal "Shaquille O'Neal")'s book, "Shaq Uncut: My Story", O'Neal responded to allegations of being a "coach killer" and that he forced Van Gundy out of Miami by stating: "Stan got fired because Pat (Riley) wanted to take over, not because I wanted him out. I had no control over it — not a smidgen of control. We all kind of knew it was coming because Pat and Stan were always arguing. Pat would come down and tell Stan how to do something and Stan would want to do it his own way, and that was a fine game plan if you wanted to get yourself fired."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-google-11)

Though at the time of his resignation Van Gundy asserted he was not being forced out by Riley, he has more recently declined comment on the situation after he accepted a coaching job with the Orlando Magic less than two years later.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-orlandosentinel-12) Riley himself would resign from his coaching duties two years later, following a 15–67 season from the Heat.

### Orlando Magic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Orlando Magic")]

In May 2007, Van Gundy received an offer to replace the fired [Rick Carlisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Carlisle "Rick Carlisle") as head coach of the [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Pacers "Indiana Pacers"). Van Gundy turned down the offer, but began interviewing for other head coaching jobs. He was considered a lead candidate to become head coach of the Orlando Magic and also the [Sacramento Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Kings "Sacramento Kings"). However, the Magic hired [Billy Donovan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Donovan "Billy Donovan"). Shortly thereafter, Donovan decided he wanted to back out of the deal and return to the [University of Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Florida "University of Florida"). Finally on June 5, 2007, the Magic released Donovan and offered another contract to Van Gundy.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-13) ESPN SportsCenter reported that the [Miami Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Heat "Miami Heat") allowed Van Gundy to coach the Magic in exchange for a second-round draft pick in 2007 and the right to swap first-round picks in 2008 or another 2008 second-round draft pick and cash.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Stan_Van_Gundy_sideline.jpg/250px-Stan_Van_Gundy_sideline.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stan_Van_Gundy_sideline.jpg)

Van Gundy coaching the Magic in 2010

In Van Gundy's first season with the Magic, he guided them to a 52-win season, earning the team's first division championship since the 1995–96 season, and the third-best record in the Eastern Conference. Orlando defeated the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors") 4–1 in the first round of the [playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_NBA_playoffs "2008 NBA playoffs"), advancing to the Eastern Semifinals for the first time in twelve seasons. They were later defeated in the Eastern Semifinals by the Detroit Pistons 4–1.

Van Gundy and the Magic won 59 games in 2008–09, the second most in franchise history, along with a second consecutive division championship finished at third place behind [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") and [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Cavaliers "Cleveland Cavaliers"). During playoffs, they defeated the [Philadelphia 76ers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_76ers "Philadelphia 76ers") from a deficit of 2–1, before squalling with Boston Celtics in seven games. Later, they defeated 66–16 Cleveland Cavaliers in the Eastern Conference finals in six games to advance to the [NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_Finals "2009 NBA Finals"), Orlando's first Finals appearance since 1995. After suffering a blowout loss in game 1 against the [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers "Los Angeles Lakers"), the Magic put up a better effort in game 2, but were defeated in overtime. In game 3, the Magic shot 63% for the game, a Finals record, en route to their first win in a Finals game in franchise history. They went on to lose the next two games, a controversial decision for allowing the four-month injury absence all-star, [Jameer Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jameer_Nelson "Jameer Nelson") to play in heavy minutes and decided not fouling the opposite team in less than 30 second in game 4, that ultimately cost them the title as the Lakers won the series in five.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Also during the 2008–09 season, a feud developed between Van Gundy and the then [Phoenix Suns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Suns "Phoenix Suns")' center, and former Magic/Heat player, [Shaquille O'Neal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaquille_O'Neal "Shaquille O'Neal") (the two were together when O'Neal played for the Heat and Van Gundy was his coach). After a game between the Suns and Magic, Van Gundy said O'Neal was [flopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flop_(basketball) "Flop (basketball)") throughout the night. O'Neal fired back by calling Van Gundy "a master of panic," because Van Gundy was not successful in the playoffs per O'Neal.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-14)

On January 31, 2010, Van Gundy was named the coach of the Eastern Conference All-Star team for the [2010 NBA All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_NBA_All-Star_Game "2010 NBA All-Star Game"), making it the second time he had been given the honor to coach an all-star team. He led the Eastern Conference to victory for the second time.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-15)

On May 21, 2012, Van Gundy was relieved of his duties as head coach.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-16) Prior to the firing, Van Gundy had stated that he had knowledge that [Dwight Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Howard "Dwight Howard") wanted him fired. Van Gundy stated that a person within management had told him this, and that the team did not want to risk angering Howard (Howard had an opt-out clause in his contract).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-17) Howard still requested a trade after the season,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] and was traded to the Los Angeles Lakers in August 2012.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-18)

### Detroit Pistons

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Detroit Pistons")]

On May 14, 2014, Van Gundy was hired as the new head coach and president of basketball operations of the [Detroit Pistons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Pistons "Detroit Pistons"), replacing interim head coach [John Loyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Loyer "John Loyer").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-vangundy-2) On February 9, 2015, Van Gundy became the 43rd coach in NBA history to win 400 games when the Pistons defeated the [Atlanta Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Hawks "Atlanta Hawks") 105–95. He clinched a berth in the [2016 playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_NBA_playoffs "2016 NBA playoffs"). On May 7, 2018, the Pistons announced that Van Gundy was released from his duties as head coach and president of basketball operations.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-19)

### New Orleans Pelicans

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: New Orleans Pelicans")]

On October 22, 2020, Van Gundy was hired as the new head coach of the [New Orleans Pelicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_Pelicans "New Orleans Pelicans"), replacing [Alvin Gentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Gentry "Alvin Gentry").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-20) Van Gundy and the Pelicans parted ways on June 16, 2021.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-21)

## Broadcasting career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Broadcasting career")]

Van Gundy became a broadcaster in September 2018, working with ESPN as an analyst for NBA games. Van Gundy left ESPN in 2019 to work for [TNT Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNT_Sports_(United_States) "TNT Sports (United States)") on NBA games.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-22) He would leave TNT after one season to become the head coach of the New Orleans Pelicans but would return to TNT one year later after he parted ways with the Pelicans. Since 2023, Van Gundy has also called [NCAA March Madness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_March_Madness_(TV_program) "NCAA March Madness (TV program)") games for TNT and [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Sports "CBS Sports").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-23) After TNT's loss of NBA rights, Van Gundy joined [Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_on_Amazon_Prime_Video "Sports on Amazon Prime Video") as a game analyst for the streaming service's [NBA coverage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_Prime "NBA on Prime"). He reunited with [Kevin Harlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Harlan "Kevin Harlan") and [Ian Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Eagle "Ian Eagle") and is working the service's conference finals coverage. Van Gundy will remain with CBS and TNT for his college basketball duty.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Van Gundy was born in [Indio, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indio,_California "Indio, California"). He grew up as a son of a basketball coach, Bill Van Gundy, the former head coach at [Brockport State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brockport_State_University "Brockport State University") in [Western New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_New_York "Western New York"). His younger brother [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy") has coached two teams in the [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") as well. After Jeff became a member of the _[NBA on ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA\_on\_ABC "NBA on ABC")'s_ broadcast team, he was an analyst during the [2009 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_Finals "2009 NBA Finals") while Stan coached the Orlando Magic.

Van Gundy has four children with his late wife Kim, who died unexpectedly in August 2023. They were married for 25 years.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-24) He revealed on a podcast that Kim died by suicide.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-26)

Van Gundy is also teaching a sports business course at Stetson University.

**Stanley Alan Van Gundy** (born August 26, 1959)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-bbr-1) is an American former [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") coach who is a television commentator for _[College Basketball on CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College\_Basketball\_on\_CBS "College Basketball on CBS")_ for [CBS Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Sports "CBS Sports") and _[NBA on Prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA\_on\_Prime "NBA on Prime")_ for [Sports on Amazon Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_on_Amazon_Prime_Video "Sports on Amazon Prime Video"). He previously worked as game analyst for [NBA on TNT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_TNT "NBA on TNT") from [2019 to 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019%E2%80%9320_NBA_season "2019–20 NBA season"), and again from [2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_NBA_season "2021–22 NBA season") to [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024%E2%80%9325_NBA_season "2024–25 NBA season"). Prior to TNT, he was most recently the head coach for the [New Orleans Pelicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_Pelicans "New Orleans Pelicans") of the NBA. He also served as the head coach and president of basketball operations for the [Detroit Pistons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Pistons "Detroit Pistons") from 2014 to 2018.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-vangundy-2) From 2003 to 2005, he was the head coach of the [Miami Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Heat "Miami Heat") but resigned in 2005 mid-season, returning the job over to [Pat Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Riley "Pat Riley"). Van Gundy then coached the Orlando Magic for five seasons from 2007 to 2012, leading them to the [2009 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_Finals "2009 NBA Finals"). He is the older brother of former [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks") and [Houston Rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Rockets "Houston Rockets") head coach [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy").

## Playing career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Playing career")]

Van Gundy was a starting guard at [Alhambra High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alhambra_High_School_(Martinez,_California) "Alhambra High School (Martinez, California)") in [Martinez, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martinez,_California "Martinez, California") in the [San Francisco Bay Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco_Bay_Area "San Francisco Bay Area"). After his senior year, he played for an all-county team that also included [Kenny Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Carter "Ken Carter"), whose coaching career was the basis for _[Coach Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coach\_Carter "Coach Carter")_, a Hollywood feature film starring [Samuel L. Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_L._Jackson "Samuel L. Jackson"). Van Gundy played college basketball for his father, [Bill Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Van_Gundy "Bill Van Gundy"), at [SUNY-Brockport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_University_of_New_York_at_Brockport "State University of New York at Brockport"), a Division III school, until he graduated in 1981 with a B.A. in English and a B.S. in Physical Education.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-heatbio-3)

## Coaching career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Coaching career")]

### College

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: College")]

Van Gundy began his coaching career as an assistant coach at the [University of Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Vermont "University of Vermont"), 1981–83, and was head coach at [Castleton State College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Castleton_State_College "Castleton State College") in Vermont for three seasons from 1983 to 1986.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-heatbio-3) After his first season as Castleton head coach, the NAIA named Van Gundy the District 5 Coach of the Year.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-Wisconsin_top_assistant-4) Castleton finished 1984–85 the top team in the [NAIA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Association_of_Intercollegiate_Athletics "National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics")'s Mayflower Conference and won the NAIA District 5 tournament.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-6) After serving as an assistant coach at [Canisius College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canisius_College "Canisius College") in 1987 and [Fordham University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fordham_University "Fordham University") in 1988, Van Gundy was named head coach at the University of Lowell. During his four-season tenure at the school, which saw the institution become the [University of Massachusetts Lowell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Massachusetts_Lowell "University of Massachusetts Lowell"), he compiled a record of 54–60 and coached Leo Parent, whom Van Gundy called "the best Division 2 player in the nation."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-7)

Van Gundy then became an assistant at the [University of Wisconsin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Madison "University of Wisconsin–Madison") under [Stu Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stu_Jackson "Stu Jackson").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-heatbio-3) When Jackson left after 2 years to become general manager of the expansion NBA Vancouver franchise, Van Gundy was promoted to replace him as head coach and given a 5-year contract. Coming off an 18–11 season with future NBA star [Michael Finley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Finley "Michael Finley") back for his senior year and highly touted recruits coming in, the team went into the season with high expectations, but ended with a disappointing 13–14 record (7–11 and ninth place in the Big 10). Van Gundy was fired at the end of the season and given a buyout for the 4 years remaining on his contract. Van Gundy blamed financial concerns at the school for his firing.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-8) The team would go on to hire [Dick Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Bennett "Dick Bennett") from the [University of Wisconsin–Green Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Wisconsin%E2%80%93Green_Bay "University of Wisconsin–Green Bay") and he finished his first year with a 17–15 record and NIT appearance despite losing Finley and other key players.

Overall, Van Gundy compiled a record of 135–92 (.595) in eight years as a college head coach.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-heatbio-3)

### Miami Heat

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Miami Heat")]

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/84/StanVanGundy_20050723_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-StanVanGundy_20050723_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:StanVanGundy_20050723_(cropped).jpg)

Van Gundy in 2005

When [Pat Riley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pat_Riley "Pat Riley") left the [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks") to coach the [Miami Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Heat "Miami Heat"), the Knicks refused to let him hire [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy"), perhaps his most valuable assistant. Riley hired Stan, his brother, saying "I wanted at least one Van Gundy with me".[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-berkow19970420-9) Stan Van Gundy spent 12 years with the Heat. After working as an assistant under Riley, Van Gundy was named head coach when Riley abruptly resigned as coach prior to the [2003–04 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003%E2%80%9304_NBA_season "2003–04 NBA season"). However, Riley remained as President of the team. Van Gundy took over a team that had won 25 games the previous season. He led them to a 42-win season, in which they won a very high percentage of their late season games and surprised many by advancing to the second round of the [2004 NBA playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_NBA_playoffs "2004 NBA playoffs"), nearly defeating the team with the league's best record, the [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Pacers "Indiana Pacers"), with Van Gundy's dynamic coaching showcasing the strong play of rookie [Dwyane Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwyane_Wade "Dwyane Wade").

During the off-season, [Shaquille O'Neal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaquille_O'Neal "Shaquille O'Neal") demanded a trade and made Miami the only viable option for the Lakers to make a transaction with. Riley gave up [Caron Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caron_Butler "Caron Butler"), [Lamar Odom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lamar_Odom "Lamar Odom"), [Brian Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Grant "Brian Grant") and a future first-round [draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_draft "NBA draft") choice, replacing three of the team's starters, including an Olympian, with O'Neal. Van Gundy led the Heat to the best record in the [Eastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Conference_(NBA) "Eastern Conference (NBA)") in the first half of the season, becoming the first Heat coach to coach in the [All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_NBA_All-Star_Game "2005 NBA All-Star Game"), where he led the East to a victory. The Heat finished the season with 59 wins, earning the best record in the conference. The Heat went on to advance to Game 7 of the Eastern Conference finals, where they lost to the [Detroit Pistons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Pistons "Detroit Pistons"). Injuries played a factor in their defeat, particularly a rib injury to leading scorer Wade during Game 5, which prevented him from playing Game 6 and severely hindered him in Game 7, both Piston wins.

During the 2005 off-season, it was widely speculated that Pat Riley was attempting to run Van Gundy out of his coaching job and take over the job himself, now that the team was in a position to contend for the championship.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-go-10) Van Gundy would resign from his position as head coach on December 12, 2005, just 21 games into the season, citing a need to spend more time with his family. Riley replaced him as head coach, and led Miami to their first championship that same season.

In [Shaquille O'Neal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaquille_O'Neal "Shaquille O'Neal")'s book, "Shaq Uncut: My Story", O'Neal responded to allegations of being a "coach killer" and that he forced Van Gundy out of Miami by stating: "Stan got fired because Pat (Riley) wanted to take over, not because I wanted him out. I had no control over it — not a smidgen of control. We all kind of knew it was coming because Pat and Stan were always arguing. Pat would come down and tell Stan how to do something and Stan would want to do it his own way, and that was a fine game plan if you wanted to get yourself fired."[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-google-11)

Though at the time of his resignation Van Gundy asserted he was not being forced out by Riley, he has more recently declined comment on the situation after he accepted a coaching job with the Orlando Magic less than two years later.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-orlandosentinel-12) Riley himself would resign from his coaching duties two years later, following a 15–67 season from the Heat.

### Orlando Magic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Orlando Magic")]

In May 2007, Van Gundy received an offer to replace the fired [Rick Carlisle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Carlisle "Rick Carlisle") as head coach of the [Indiana Pacers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Pacers "Indiana Pacers"). Van Gundy turned down the offer, but began interviewing for other head coaching jobs. He was considered a lead candidate to become head coach of the Orlando Magic and also the [Sacramento Kings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento_Kings "Sacramento Kings"). However, the Magic hired [Billy Donovan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billy_Donovan "Billy Donovan"). Shortly thereafter, Donovan decided he wanted to back out of the deal and return to the [University of Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Florida "University of Florida"). Finally on June 5, 2007, the Magic released Donovan and offered another contract to Van Gundy.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-13) ESPN SportsCenter reported that the [Miami Heat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miami_Heat "Miami Heat") allowed Van Gundy to coach the Magic in exchange for a second-round draft pick in 2007 and the right to swap first-round picks in 2008 or another 2008 second-round draft pick and cash.

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/06/Stan_Van_Gundy_sideline.jpg/250px-Stan_Van_Gundy_sideline.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Stan_Van_Gundy_sideline.jpg)

Van Gundy coaching the Magic in 2010

In Van Gundy's first season with the Magic, he guided them to a 52-win season, earning the team's first division championship since the 1995–96 season, and the third-best record in the Eastern Conference. Orlando defeated the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors") 4–1 in the first round of the [playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_NBA_playoffs "2008 NBA playoffs"), advancing to the Eastern Semifinals for the first time in twelve seasons. They were later defeated in the Eastern Semifinals by the Detroit Pistons 4–1.

Van Gundy and the Magic won 59 games in 2008–09, the second most in franchise history, along with a second consecutive division championship finished at third place behind [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") and [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Cavaliers "Cleveland Cavaliers"). During playoffs, they defeated the [Philadelphia 76ers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_76ers "Philadelphia 76ers") from a deficit of 2–1, before squalling with Boston Celtics in seven games. Later, they defeated 66–16 Cleveland Cavaliers in the Eastern Conference finals in six games to advance to the [NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_Finals "2009 NBA Finals"), Orlando's first Finals appearance since 1995. After suffering a blowout loss in game 1 against the [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers "Los Angeles Lakers"), the Magic put up a better effort in game 2, but were defeated in overtime. In game 3, the Magic shot 63% for the game, a Finals record, en route to their first win in a Finals game in franchise history. They went on to lose the next two games, a controversial decision for allowing the four-month injury absence all-star, [Jameer Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jameer_Nelson "Jameer Nelson") to play in heavy minutes and decided not fouling the opposite team in less than 30 second in game 4, that ultimately cost them the title as the Lakers won the series in five.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Also during the 2008–09 season, a feud developed between Van Gundy and the then [Phoenix Suns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Suns "Phoenix Suns")' center, and former Magic/Heat player, [Shaquille O'Neal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaquille_O'Neal "Shaquille O'Neal") (the two were together when O'Neal played for the Heat and Van Gundy was his coach). After a game between the Suns and Magic, Van Gundy said O'Neal was [flopping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flop_(basketball) "Flop (basketball)") throughout the night. O'Neal fired back by calling Van Gundy "a master of panic," because Van Gundy was not successful in the playoffs per O'Neal.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-14)

On January 31, 2010, Van Gundy was named the coach of the Eastern Conference All-Star team for the [2010 NBA All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_NBA_All-Star_Game "2010 NBA All-Star Game"), making it the second time he had been given the honor to coach an all-star team. He led the Eastern Conference to victory for the second time.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-15)

On May 21, 2012, Van Gundy was relieved of his duties as head coach.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-16) Prior to the firing, Van Gundy had stated that he had knowledge that [Dwight Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Howard "Dwight Howard") wanted him fired. Van Gundy stated that a person within management had told him this, and that the team did not want to risk angering Howard (Howard had an opt-out clause in his contract).[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-17) Howard still requested a trade after the season,[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] and was traded to the Los Angeles Lakers in August 2012.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-18)

### Detroit Pistons

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Detroit Pistons")]

On May 14, 2014, Van Gundy was hired as the new head coach and president of basketball operations of the [Detroit Pistons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Pistons "Detroit Pistons"), replacing interim head coach [John Loyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Loyer "John Loyer").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-vangundy-2) On February 9, 2015, Van Gundy became the 43rd coach in NBA history to win 400 games when the Pistons defeated the [Atlanta Hawks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta_Hawks "Atlanta Hawks") 105–95. He clinched a berth in the [2016 playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_NBA_playoffs "2016 NBA playoffs"). On May 7, 2018, the Pistons announced that Van Gundy was released from his duties as head coach and president of basketball operations.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-19)

### New Orleans Pelicans

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: New Orleans Pelicans")]

On October 22, 2020, Van Gundy was hired as the new head coach of the [New Orleans Pelicans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Orleans_Pelicans "New Orleans Pelicans"), replacing [Alvin Gentry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Gentry "Alvin Gentry").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-20) Van Gundy and the Pelicans parted ways on June 16, 2021.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-21)

## Broadcasting career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Broadcasting career")]

Van Gundy became a broadcaster in September 2018, working with ESPN as an analyst for NBA games. Van Gundy left ESPN in 2019 to work for [TNT Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TNT_Sports_(United_States) "TNT Sports (United States)") on NBA games.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-22) He would leave TNT after one season to become the head coach of the New Orleans Pelicans but would return to TNT one year later after he parted ways with the Pelicans. Since 2023, Van Gundy has also called [NCAA March Madness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_March_Madness_(TV_program) "NCAA March Madness (TV program)") games for TNT and [CBS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBS_Sports "CBS Sports").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-23) After TNT's loss of NBA rights, Van Gundy joined [Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_on_Amazon_Prime_Video "Sports on Amazon Prime Video") as a game analyst for the streaming service's [NBA coverage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_on_Prime "NBA on Prime"). He reunited with [Kevin Harlan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevin_Harlan "Kevin Harlan") and [Ian Eagle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Eagle "Ian Eagle") and is working the service's conference finals coverage. Van Gundy will remain with CBS and TNT for his college basketball duty.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stan_Van_Gundy&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Van Gundy was born in [Indio, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indio,_California "Indio, California"). He grew up as a son of a basketball coach, Bill Van Gundy, the former head coach at [Brockport State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brockport_State_University "Brockport State University") in [Western New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_New_York "Western New York"). His younger brother [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy") has coached two teams in the [NBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") as well. After Jeff became a member of the _[NBA on ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA\_on\_ABC "NBA on ABC")'s_ broadcast team, he was an analyst during the [2009 NBA Finals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_NBA_Finals "2009 NBA Finals") while Stan coached the Orlando Magic.

Van Gundy has four children with his late wife Kim, who died unexpectedly in August 2023. They were married for 25 years.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-24) He revealed on a podcast that Kim died by suicide.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stan_Van_Gundy#cite_note-26)

Van Gundy is also teaching a sports business course at Stetson University.

**Douglas Harry Wheelock** (born May 5, 1960) is an American [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer") and [astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). He has flown in space twice, logging 178 days on the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle"), [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"), and Russian [Soyuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(spacecraft) "Soyuz (spacecraft)"). On July 12, 2011, Wheelock announced that he would be returning to active duty with the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") in support of [Operation Enduring Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Enduring_Freedom "Operation Enduring Freedom").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-3) He is currently working with [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") to test the [Orion spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_spacecraft "Orion spacecraft") at the [Glenn Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Research_Center "Glenn Research Center") in Plum Brook, Ohio.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-magill-4)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Douglas Wheelock was born in [Binghamton, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binghamton,_New_York "Binghamton, New York"), to Olin and Margaret Wheelock. In a pre-flight interview, Wheelock stated that he was inspired to become an astronaut at an early age. He also stated that a major turning point in his life was the [Apollo 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11 "Apollo 11") Moon landing in July 1969.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-preflight-5) In 1978 Wheelock graduated from Windsor Central High School in [Windsor, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor_(town),_New_York "Windsor (town), New York"), before attending the [United States Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy "United States Military Academy") at [West Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point,_New_York "West Point, New York").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-bio-6) He earned a Master of Science degree in Aerospace Engineering at [Georgia Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Institute_of_Technology "Georgia Institute of Technology") in 1992.

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

Wheelock spent four years as a cadet at West Point, graduating in the class of 1983 with a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [applied science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_science "Applied science") and [engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering "Engineering"). After graduation he was commissioned a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_lieutenant "Second lieutenant") in the U.S. Army's [Infantry Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infantry_Branch_(United_States) "Infantry Branch (United States)") and entered flight school the next year. In September 1984, then Lieutenant Wheelock graduated at the top of his flight class and was designated an [army aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Aviator_Badge "United States Aviator Badge"). He subsequently served in the Pacific as a combat aviation section leader, platoon leader, company executive officer, battalion operations officer, and commander of an air cavalry troop in the [9th Cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_Cavalry_Regiment_(United_States) "9th Cavalry Regiment (United States)"). He was later assigned to the Aviation Directorate of Combat Developments as an advanced weapons research and development engineer.

Wheelock was selected as a member of Class 104 at the [U.S. Naval Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Test_Pilot_School "U.S. Naval Test Pilot School") and upon completion was assigned as an experimental test pilot with the Army Aviation Technical Test Center (ATTC). His flight testing was focused in the areas of tactical reconnaissance and surveillance systems in the [OH-58D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OH-58D "OH-58D"), [UH-60](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UH-60 "UH-60"), [RU-21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RU-21 "RU-21") and [C-23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-23_Sherpa "C-23 Sherpa") aircraft. He served as division chief for fixed-wing testing of airborne signal and imagery intelligence systems in support of the National Program Office for Intelligence and Electronic Warfare.

While on active duty, Wheelock received a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in [aerospace engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_engineering "Aerospace engineering") from [Georgia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Tech "Georgia Tech") in 1992. In August 1996 Wheelock was assigned to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") as a Space Shuttle integration test engineer. His technical duties involved engineering liaison for launch and landing operations of the Space Shuttle. He was selected as the vehicle integration test team lead for the joint Space Shuttle and Russian Space Station _[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")_ mission [STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86"), and lead engineer for International Space Station hardware fit checks.

Wheelock is a graduate of the Army Airborne and Air Assault Courses, the Infantry and Aviation Officer Advanced Courses, the Combined Arms Services Staff School, the Material Acquisition Management Course, and the [U.S. Army Command and General Staff College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Command_and_General_Staff_College "U.S. Army Command and General Staff College"). In July 2011, Wheelock left for a tour of duty in support of Operation Enduring Freedom. A dual-rated master army aviator astronaut, he has logged over 2,500 flight hours in 43 different rotary and fixed-wing aircraft.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-bio-6)

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Douglas_H._Wheelock.jpg/250px-Douglas_H._Wheelock.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Douglas_H._Wheelock.jpg)

Wheelock's astronaut candidate photo

In August 1998 Wheelock reported for [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") astronaut candidate training. Having completed the initial two years of intensive Space Shuttle and Space Station training, he was assigned to the Astronaut Office ISS Operations Branch as a Russian Liaison, participating in the testing and integration of Russian hardware and software products developed for the ISS. He worked extensively with the Energia Aerospace Company in [Moscow, Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow,_Russia "Moscow, Russia"), developing and verifying dual-language procedures for ISS crews. Wheelock led joint U.S./Russian teams to the [Baikonur Cosmodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikonur_Cosmodrome "Baikonur Cosmodrome") in [Kazakhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan "Kazakhstan") to oversee bench reviews, inventory, loading and launch of the first four uncrewed ISS resupply capsules.

In 2001, Wheelock assumed duties as the crew support astronaut for the ISS [Expedition 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_2 "Expedition 2") crew, which was in orbit for 147 days from March 2001 to August 2001, and for the ISS [Expedition 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_4 "Expedition 4") crew, which was on orbit for 195 days from December 2001 to June 2002. He was the primary contact for all crew needs, coordination, planning and interactions, and was the primary representative of the crews while they were in orbit. In August 2002, Wheelock was assigned as a spacecraft communicator ([CAPCOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller#Spacecraft_communicator_(CAPCOM) "Flight controller")) in the Mission Control Center in [Houston, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas"). In this role, he was the primary communication link between crews in orbit and the ground support team in the Control Center. His work as a CAPCOM culminated in his assignment as the lead CAPCOM for the ISS [Expedition 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_8 "Expedition 8") mission, which was 194 days in duration.

In July 2004, Wheelock served as an [aquanaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquanaut "Aquanaut") during the [NEEMO 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEEMO#NEEMO_6:_July_12%E2%80%9321,_2004 "NEEMO") mission aboard the [Aquarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarius_(laboratory) "Aquarius (laboratory)")[underwater laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_habitat "Underwater habitat"), living and working underwater for ten days.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-six-7)

In January 2005 and again in 2016, he was assigned as NASA's Director of Operations – Russia where he served at the [Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gagarin_Cosmonaut_Training_Center "Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center") in [Star City, Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City,_Russia "Star City, Russia"). He was responsible for supporting Russia-based training, logistic, and administrative needs of NASA astronauts preparing for flight on the ISS. Wheelock was the primary liaison between Star City and NASA operations in Houston, including medical, training, science, contracting, public affairs, and administration departments. He was also responsible for liaison duties between NASA and the [Russian Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Space_Agency "Russian Space Agency"), as well as the Russian aerospace industry.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-bio-6)

After his first spaceflight, Wheelock was assigned as the backup to [T.J. Creamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Creamer "Timothy Creamer") for the [Soyuz TMA-17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TMA-17 "Soyuz TMA-17")/[Expedition 22](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_22 "Expedition 22")/[Expedition 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_23 "Expedition 23") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). Creamer completed a successful 163-day mission from 2009 to 2010.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-8)

As of September 2019, Wheelock was working as an astronaut trainer testing systems aboard the [Orion spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_spacecraft "Orion spacecraft").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-magill-4) That month, he contributed to an article in _[The Columbus Dispatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Columbus\_Dispatch "The Columbus Dispatch")_ detailing the inaccuracies of the space science fiction film _[Ad Astra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad\_Astra\_(film) "Ad Astra (film)")_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-burger-9)

### Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

#### STS-120

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: STS-120")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Doug_Wheelock-STS-120.jpg/250px-Doug_Wheelock-STS-120.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Doug_Wheelock-STS-120.jpg)

Wheelock working on the outside of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") during STS-120

On October 23, 2007, Wheelock launched on his first spaceflight aboard [Space Shuttle _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery"). During the STS-120 mission, Wheelock was [Mission Specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Specialist "Mission Specialist") 3 on a multinational crew whose mission was to deliver the [Node 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node_2 "Node 2") module to the International Space Station. Wheelock participated in three [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalks "Spacewalks") with fellow astronaut [Scott Parazynski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Parazynski "Scott Parazynski") in order to perform mission critical tasks on the exterior of the Station. The spacewalks involved outfitting the Node 2 module, storing an S-band antenna, work on the [Integrated Truss Structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure "Integrated Truss Structure"), and [External Stowage Platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_Stowage_Platform "External Stowage Platform") 2. During the mission a solar array on the P6 truss tore requiring an emergency repair by Wheelock and Parazynski. Parazynski attached cufflinks to the solar array allowing it to expand without additional damage. Wheelock orbited the Earth 238 times during the 15-day mission.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-10)

#### Expedition 24/25

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Expedition 24/25")]

Wheelock launched to the International Space Station on June 15, 2010, aboard the [Soyuz TMA-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TMA-19 "Soyuz TMA-19") spacecraft with [Fyodor Yurchikhin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyodor_Yurchikhin "Fyodor Yurchikhin") and [Shannon Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon_Walker "Shannon Walker").

Wheelock joined the [Expedition 24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_24 "Expedition 24") crew in progress.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-Hires24-11) During the mission he participated in several scientific investigations. On July 31, 2010, a pump module on the exterior of the Space Station failed. Wheelock and [Tracy Caldwell-Dyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracy_Caldwell-Dyson "Tracy Caldwell-Dyson") made three spacewalks to replace the module, during which he sustained long-term damage to his vision.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-AmmoniaPump-12)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-burger-9) The failed pump module was later returned home on [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-13)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Soyuz_TMA-19_Crew_in_front_of_the_capsule_%28closeup%29.jpg/250px-Soyuz_TMA-19_Crew_in_front_of_the_capsule_%28closeup%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Soyuz_TMA-19_Crew_in_front_of_the_capsule_(closeup).jpg)

Wheelock and his crewmates outside their Soyuz spacecraft

On September 22, 2010, Wheelock took command of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") at the beginning of [Expedition 25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_25 "Expedition 25").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-14) He is the first U.S. Army officer to command the ISS.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-15) Wheelock and his crew continued science and maintenance of the space station. Wheelock is sharing pictures of the Earth, station and views of space via [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter"), as [Soichi Noguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soichi_Noguchi "Soichi Noguchi") did before him.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-16) In September 2010, Wheelock tweeted photos from space of [Hurricane Earl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Earl_(2010) "Hurricane Earl (2010)").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-New_York_Daily_News-17) He also participated in a [NASA Tweetup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Tweetup "NASA Tweetup") on March 16, 2011.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-18)

He became the first person to "check in" from space on October 22, using the mobile social networking application [Foursquare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foursquare_City_Guide "Foursquare City Guide"). Wheelock's check-in to the International Space Station launched a partnership between NASA and Foursquare to connect its users to the space agency, enabling them to explore the universe and discover Earth.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-NASA-19)

He returned to Earth on November 26, 2010, aboard the Soyuz.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Personal life")]

His hometown is Windsor, New York. Wheelock's parents, Olin and Margaret Wheelock, reside in upstate New York.

In 1989 he was selected by the U.S. [Jaycees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaycees "Jaycees") as one of "Ten Outstanding Young Men of America". In 1990 the [Veterans of Foreign Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterans_of_Foreign_Wars "Veterans of Foreign Wars") selected Wheelock as an "Outstanding Spokesman for Freedom".

### Organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Organizations")]

Wheelock is a member of the [Society of Experimental Test Pilots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Experimental_Test_Pilots "Society of Experimental Test Pilots"), the [Society of American Military Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_American_Military_Engineers "Society of American Military Engineers"), the [Association of the United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_the_United_States_Army "Association of the United States Army"), and the [Army Aviation Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Aviation_Association_of_America?action=edit&redlink=1 "Army Aviation Association of America (page does not exist)").
