**Douglas Harry Wheelock** (born May 5, 1960) is an American [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer") and [astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). He has flown in space twice, logging 178 days on the [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle"), [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"), and Russian [Soyuz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_(spacecraft) "Soyuz (spacecraft)"). On July 12, 2011, Wheelock announced that he would be returning to active duty with the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") in support of [Operation Enduring Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Enduring_Freedom "Operation Enduring Freedom").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-3) He is currently working with [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") to test the [Orion spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_spacecraft "Orion spacecraft") at the [Glenn Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Research_Center "Glenn Research Center") in Plum Brook, Ohio.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-magill-4)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Douglas Wheelock was born in [Binghamton, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Binghamton,_New_York "Binghamton, New York"), to Olin and Margaret Wheelock. In a pre-flight interview, Wheelock stated that he was inspired to become an astronaut at an early age. He also stated that a major turning point in his life was the [Apollo 11](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_11 "Apollo 11") Moon landing in July 1969.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-preflight-5) In 1978 Wheelock graduated from Windsor Central High School in [Windsor, New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windsor_(town),_New_York "Windsor (town), New York"), before attending the [United States Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy "United States Military Academy") at [West Point](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point,_New_York "West Point, New York").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-bio-6) He earned a Master of Science degree in Aerospace Engineering at [Georgia Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Institute_of_Technology "Georgia Institute of Technology") in 1992.

## Military career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Military career")]

Wheelock spent four years as a cadet at West Point, graduating in the class of 1983 with a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [applied science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_science "Applied science") and [engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering "Engineering"). After graduation he was commissioned a [second lieutenant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_lieutenant "Second lieutenant") in the U.S. Army's [Infantry Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Infantry_Branch_(United_States) "Infantry Branch (United States)") and entered flight school the next year. In September 1984, then Lieutenant Wheelock graduated at the top of his flight class and was designated an [army aviator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Aviator_Badge "United States Aviator Badge"). He subsequently served in the Pacific as a combat aviation section leader, platoon leader, company executive officer, battalion operations officer, and commander of an air cavalry troop in the [9th Cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/9th_Cavalry_Regiment_(United_States) "9th Cavalry Regiment (United States)"). He was later assigned to the Aviation Directorate of Combat Developments as an advanced weapons research and development engineer.

Wheelock was selected as a member of Class 104 at the [U.S. Naval Test Pilot School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Naval_Test_Pilot_School "U.S. Naval Test Pilot School") and upon completion was assigned as an experimental test pilot with the Army Aviation Technical Test Center (ATTC). His flight testing was focused in the areas of tactical reconnaissance and surveillance systems in the [OH-58D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OH-58D "OH-58D"), [UH-60](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UH-60 "UH-60"), [RU-21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RU-21 "RU-21") and [C-23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-23_Sherpa "C-23 Sherpa") aircraft. He served as division chief for fixed-wing testing of airborne signal and imagery intelligence systems in support of the National Program Office for Intelligence and Electronic Warfare.

While on active duty, Wheelock received a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in [aerospace engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_engineering "Aerospace engineering") from [Georgia Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Tech "Georgia Tech") in 1992. In August 1996 Wheelock was assigned to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") as a Space Shuttle integration test engineer. His technical duties involved engineering liaison for launch and landing operations of the Space Shuttle. He was selected as the vehicle integration test team lead for the joint Space Shuttle and Russian Space Station _[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir")_ mission [STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86"), and lead engineer for International Space Station hardware fit checks.

Wheelock is a graduate of the Army Airborne and Air Assault Courses, the Infantry and Aviation Officer Advanced Courses, the Combined Arms Services Staff School, the Material Acquisition Management Course, and the [U.S. Army Command and General Staff College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Command_and_General_Staff_College "U.S. Army Command and General Staff College"). In July 2011, Wheelock left for a tour of duty in support of Operation Enduring Freedom. A dual-rated master army aviator astronaut, he has logged over 2,500 flight hours in 43 different rotary and fixed-wing aircraft.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-bio-6)

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: NASA career")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Douglas_H._Wheelock.jpg/250px-Douglas_H._Wheelock.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Douglas_H._Wheelock.jpg)

Wheelock's astronaut candidate photo

In August 1998 Wheelock reported for [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") astronaut candidate training. Having completed the initial two years of intensive Space Shuttle and Space Station training, he was assigned to the Astronaut Office ISS Operations Branch as a Russian Liaison, participating in the testing and integration of Russian hardware and software products developed for the ISS. He worked extensively with the Energia Aerospace Company in [Moscow, Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow,_Russia "Moscow, Russia"), developing and verifying dual-language procedures for ISS crews. Wheelock led joint U.S./Russian teams to the [Baikonur Cosmodrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baikonur_Cosmodrome "Baikonur Cosmodrome") in [Kazakhstan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kazakhstan "Kazakhstan") to oversee bench reviews, inventory, loading and launch of the first four uncrewed ISS resupply capsules.

In 2001, Wheelock assumed duties as the crew support astronaut for the ISS [Expedition 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_2 "Expedition 2") crew, which was in orbit for 147 days from March 2001 to August 2001, and for the ISS [Expedition 4](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_4 "Expedition 4") crew, which was on orbit for 195 days from December 2001 to June 2002. He was the primary contact for all crew needs, coordination, planning and interactions, and was the primary representative of the crews while they were in orbit. In August 2002, Wheelock was assigned as a spacecraft communicator ([CAPCOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller#Spacecraft_communicator_(CAPCOM) "Flight controller")) in the Mission Control Center in [Houston, Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston,_Texas "Houston, Texas"). In this role, he was the primary communication link between crews in orbit and the ground support team in the Control Center. His work as a CAPCOM culminated in his assignment as the lead CAPCOM for the ISS [Expedition 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_8 "Expedition 8") mission, which was 194 days in duration.

In July 2004, Wheelock served as an [aquanaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquanaut "Aquanaut") during the [NEEMO 6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NEEMO#NEEMO_6:_July_12%E2%80%9321,_2004 "NEEMO") mission aboard the [Aquarius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarius_(laboratory) "Aquarius (laboratory)")[underwater laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Underwater_habitat "Underwater habitat"), living and working underwater for ten days.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-six-7)

In January 2005 and again in 2016, he was assigned as NASA's Director of Operations – Russia where he served at the [Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gagarin_Cosmonaut_Training_Center "Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center") in [Star City, Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City,_Russia "Star City, Russia"). He was responsible for supporting Russia-based training, logistic, and administrative needs of NASA astronauts preparing for flight on the ISS. Wheelock was the primary liaison between Star City and NASA operations in Houston, including medical, training, science, contracting, public affairs, and administration departments. He was also responsible for liaison duties between NASA and the [Russian Space Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Space_Agency "Russian Space Agency"), as well as the Russian aerospace industry.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-bio-6)

After his first spaceflight, Wheelock was assigned as the backup to [T.J. Creamer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timothy_Creamer "Timothy Creamer") for the [Soyuz TMA-17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TMA-17 "Soyuz TMA-17")/[Expedition 22](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_22 "Expedition 22")/[Expedition 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_23 "Expedition 23") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station"). Creamer completed a successful 163-day mission from 2009 to 2010.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-8)

As of September 2019, Wheelock was working as an astronaut trainer testing systems aboard the [Orion spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orion_spacecraft "Orion spacecraft").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-magill-4) That month, he contributed to an article in _[The Columbus Dispatch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Columbus\_Dispatch "The Columbus Dispatch")_ detailing the inaccuracies of the space science fiction film _[Ad Astra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ad\_Astra\_(film) "Ad Astra (film)")_.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-burger-9)

### Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

#### STS-120

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: STS-120")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0d/Doug_Wheelock-STS-120.jpg/250px-Doug_Wheelock-STS-120.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Doug_Wheelock-STS-120.jpg)

Wheelock working on the outside of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") during STS-120

On October 23, 2007, Wheelock launched on his first spaceflight aboard [Space Shuttle _Discovery_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery"). During the STS-120 mission, Wheelock was [Mission Specialist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mission_Specialist "Mission Specialist") 3 on a multinational crew whose mission was to deliver the [Node 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node_2 "Node 2") module to the International Space Station. Wheelock participated in three [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalks "Spacewalks") with fellow astronaut [Scott Parazynski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Parazynski "Scott Parazynski") in order to perform mission critical tasks on the exterior of the Station. The spacewalks involved outfitting the Node 2 module, storing an S-band antenna, work on the [Integrated Truss Structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure "Integrated Truss Structure"), and [External Stowage Platform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_Stowage_Platform "External Stowage Platform") 2. During the mission a solar array on the P6 truss tore requiring an emergency repair by Wheelock and Parazynski. Parazynski attached cufflinks to the solar array allowing it to expand without additional damage. Wheelock orbited the Earth 238 times during the 15-day mission.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-10)

#### Expedition 24/25

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Expedition 24/25")]

Wheelock launched to the International Space Station on June 15, 2010, aboard the [Soyuz TMA-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_TMA-19 "Soyuz TMA-19") spacecraft with [Fyodor Yurchikhin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fyodor_Yurchikhin "Fyodor Yurchikhin") and [Shannon Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shannon_Walker "Shannon Walker").

Wheelock joined the [Expedition 24](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_24 "Expedition 24") crew in progress.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-Hires24-11) During the mission he participated in several scientific investigations. On July 31, 2010, a pump module on the exterior of the Space Station failed. Wheelock and [Tracy Caldwell-Dyson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tracy_Caldwell-Dyson "Tracy Caldwell-Dyson") made three spacewalks to replace the module, during which he sustained long-term damage to his vision.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-AmmoniaPump-12)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-burger-9) The failed pump module was later returned home on [STS-135](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-135 "STS-135").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-13)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Soyuz_TMA-19_Crew_in_front_of_the_capsule_%28closeup%29.jpg/250px-Soyuz_TMA-19_Crew_in_front_of_the_capsule_%28closeup%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Soyuz_TMA-19_Crew_in_front_of_the_capsule_(closeup).jpg)

Wheelock and his crewmates outside their Soyuz spacecraft

On September 22, 2010, Wheelock took command of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") at the beginning of [Expedition 25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_25 "Expedition 25").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-14) He is the first U.S. Army officer to command the ISS.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-15) Wheelock and his crew continued science and maintenance of the space station. Wheelock is sharing pictures of the Earth, station and views of space via [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter"), as [Soichi Noguchi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soichi_Noguchi "Soichi Noguchi") did before him.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-16) In September 2010, Wheelock tweeted photos from space of [Hurricane Earl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurricane_Earl_(2010) "Hurricane Earl (2010)").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-New_York_Daily_News-17) He also participated in a [NASA Tweetup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Tweetup "NASA Tweetup") on March 16, 2011.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-18)

He became the first person to "check in" from space on October 22, using the mobile social networking application [Foursquare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foursquare_City_Guide "Foursquare City Guide"). Wheelock's check-in to the International Space Station launched a partnership between NASA and Foursquare to connect its users to the space agency, enabling them to explore the universe and discover Earth.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Douglas_H._Wheelock#cite_note-NASA-19)

He returned to Earth on November 26, 2010, aboard the Soyuz.

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Personal life")]

His hometown is Windsor, New York. Wheelock's parents, Olin and Margaret Wheelock, reside in upstate New York.

In 1989 he was selected by the U.S. [Jaycees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaycees "Jaycees") as one of "Ten Outstanding Young Men of America". In 1990 the [Veterans of Foreign Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterans_of_Foreign_Wars "Veterans of Foreign Wars") selected Wheelock as an "Outstanding Spokesman for Freedom".

### Organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Douglas_H._Wheelock&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Organizations")]

Wheelock is a member of the [Society of Experimental Test Pilots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_Experimental_Test_Pilots "Society of Experimental Test Pilots"), the [Society of American Military Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Society_of_American_Military_Engineers "Society of American Military Engineers"), the [Association of the United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_the_United_States_Army "Association of the United States Army"), and the [Army Aviation Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Army_Aviation_Association_of_America?action=edit&redlink=1 "Army Aviation Association of America (page does not exist)").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The Orlando Magic are an [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans "Americans") professional [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") team based in [Orlando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando,_Florida "Orlando, Florida"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). They play in the [Southeast Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Division_(NBA) "Southeast Division (NBA)") of the [Eastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Conference_(NBA) "Eastern Conference (NBA)") in the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA). The franchise was founded in 1989 as an expansion team, and plays at the [Kia Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kia_Center "Kia Center"). The team is owned by Orlando Magic, Ltd., a subsidiary of [RDV Sports, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDV_Sports,_Inc. "RDV Sports, Inc.")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-1) The team has won eight division titles (1995, 1996, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2019, 2024, 2025), two conference titles (1995, 2009), but no league championships.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-2)

There have been thirteen [head coaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_coach "Head coach") for the Magic franchise.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-3) The team's first head coach was [Matt Guokas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Guokas "Matt Guokas"), who coached the team for 328 games over four seasons.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-guokas-4)[Brian Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Hill_(basketball_coach) "Brian Hill (basketball coach)") is the team's all-time leader in regular-season games coached (459).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-hill-5) Hill is also the team's all-time leader in regular-season games won (267), and he is the team's only coach to have coached during two non-consecutive periods.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-hill-5)Stan Van Gundy was the team's coach from the beginning of the [2007–08 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007%E2%80%9308_NBA_season "2007–08 NBA season") until the end of the [2011–12 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_NBA_season "2011–12 NBA season"). He is the team's all-time leader in playoff games coached (59), playoff games won (31), regular-season [winning percentage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winning_percentage "Winning percentage") (.657), and playoff winning percentage (.523).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-gundy-6)[Doc Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers "Doc Rivers") is the team's only coach to have won the [NBA Coach of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Coach_of_the_Year "NBA Coach of the Year") award, winning it after the [1999–2000 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999%E2%80%932000_NBA_season "1999–2000 NBA season").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-coty-7)[Chris Jent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Jent "Chris Jent") is the team's only head coach to have spent his entire career with the Magic.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-jent-8)

On July 28, 2012, [Jacque Vaughn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacque_Vaughn "Jacque Vaughn") was named the new head coach. He was the assistant coach for the [San Antonio Spurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio_Spurs "San Antonio Spurs") in the two seasons prior to his hiring.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-9)

On May 29, 2015, the Magic hired their former point guard [Scott Skiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Skiles "Scott Skiles") as the franchise's 12th head coach.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-10)

When Skiles resigned after one season, the Magic hired [Frank Vogel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Vogel "Frank Vogel") as his successor.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-11) Vogel was fired following the end of the [2017–18 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_NBA_season "2017–18 NBA season"). [Steve Clifford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford "Steve Clifford") succeeded Vogel, coaching until the end of the 2020-21 season.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-12)[Jamahl Mosley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamahl_Mosley "Jamahl Mosley") took over the team after that, where he won two division championships and made three playoff appearances in five seasons. After the Magic were eliminated from the 2025-26 playoffs, Mosley was fired.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

The Orlando Magic are an [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Americans "Americans") professional [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") team based in [Orlando](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orlando,_Florida "Orlando, Florida"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"). They play in the [Southeast Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Division_(NBA) "Southeast Division (NBA)") of the [Eastern Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Conference_(NBA) "Eastern Conference (NBA)") in the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA). The franchise was founded in 1989 as an expansion team, and plays at the [Kia Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kia_Center "Kia Center"). The team is owned by Orlando Magic, Ltd., a subsidiary of [RDV Sports, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RDV_Sports,_Inc. "RDV Sports, Inc.")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-1) The team has won eight division titles (1995, 1996, 2008, 2009, 2010, 2019, 2024, 2025), two conference titles (1995, 2009), but no league championships.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-2)

There have been thirteen [head coaches](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_coach "Head coach") for the Magic franchise.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-3) The team's first head coach was [Matt Guokas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Guokas "Matt Guokas"), who coached the team for 328 games over four seasons.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-guokas-4)[Brian Hill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Hill_(basketball_coach) "Brian Hill (basketball coach)") is the team's all-time leader in regular-season games coached (459).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-hill-5) Hill is also the team's all-time leader in regular-season games won (267), and he is the team's only coach to have coached during two non-consecutive periods.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-hill-5)Stan Van Gundy was the team's coach from the beginning of the [2007–08 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007%E2%80%9308_NBA_season "2007–08 NBA season") until the end of the [2011–12 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_NBA_season "2011–12 NBA season"). He is the team's all-time leader in playoff games coached (59), playoff games won (31), regular-season [winning percentage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winning_percentage "Winning percentage") (.657), and playoff winning percentage (.523).[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-gundy-6)[Doc Rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doc_Rivers "Doc Rivers") is the team's only coach to have won the [NBA Coach of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Coach_of_the_Year "NBA Coach of the Year") award, winning it after the [1999–2000 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999%E2%80%932000_NBA_season "1999–2000 NBA season").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-coty-7)[Chris Jent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Jent "Chris Jent") is the team's only head coach to have spent his entire career with the Magic.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-jent-8)

On July 28, 2012, [Jacque Vaughn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacque_Vaughn "Jacque Vaughn") was named the new head coach. He was the assistant coach for the [San Antonio Spurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Antonio_Spurs "San Antonio Spurs") in the two seasons prior to his hiring.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-9)

On May 29, 2015, the Magic hired their former point guard [Scott Skiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Skiles "Scott Skiles") as the franchise's 12th head coach.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-10)

When Skiles resigned after one season, the Magic hired [Frank Vogel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Vogel "Frank Vogel") as his successor.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-11) Vogel was fired following the end of the [2017–18 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_NBA_season "2017–18 NBA season"). [Steve Clifford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford "Steve Clifford") succeeded Vogel, coaching until the end of the 2020-21 season.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Orlando_Magic_head_coaches#cite_note-12)[Jamahl Mosley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamahl_Mosley "Jamahl Mosley") took over the team after that, where he won two division championships and made three playoff appearances in five seasons. After the Magic were eliminated from the 2025-26 playoffs, Mosley was fired.

**Jeff Weltman** is an American [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") executive who is the president of basketball operations for the Orlando Magic of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-1)

In 2020, Weltman received one 1st place vote for [NBA Executive of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Executive_of_the_Year "NBA Executive of the Year").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-3)

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeff_Weltman&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Weltman grew up in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). He was raised by his father, [Harry Weltman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Weltman "Harry Weltman"), and his mother, Arlene. Harry Weltman was a former GM for the now defunct [ABA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Basketball_Association "American Basketball Association")'s [Spirits of St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirits_of_St._Louis "Spirits of St. Louis") in the mid-1970s and for the [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Cavaliers "Cleveland Cavaliers") and [New Jersey Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Nets "New Jersey Nets") in the mid-1980s. As a teenager, Weltman played pick-up basketball in the [South Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bronx "South Bronx") and [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem") on Saturdays. Weltman played basketball at [Oberlin College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberlin_College "Oberlin College") in Ohio.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-4)

At the start of Weltman's career, he was hired by the Clippers as a video coordinator in the late 1990s. Weltman then served as the director of player personnel with the [Los Angeles Clippers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Clippers "Los Angeles Clippers"), director of basketball administration with the [Detroit Pistons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Pistons "Detroit Pistons"), assistant GM with the [Denver Nuggets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Nuggets "Denver Nuggets") and [Milwaukee Bucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee_Bucks "Milwaukee Bucks") and EVP of basketball operations and GM with the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-6) Before Weltman joined the Raptors, the Raptors were on a five-year playoff-drought. During Weltman's four-year tenure with the Raptors, the team qualified for the postseason every season and won three playoff series. He then was offered the job of President of Basketball Operations for the Orlando Magic. He took the position and moved to Orlando with his wife, Alexis, and his twin daughters, JJ and Lucy.

## Orlando Magic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeff_Weltman&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Orlando Magic")]

On April 13, 2017, the Magic fired GM [Rob Hennigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Hennigan "Rob Hennigan") and assistant GM [Scott Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Perry_(basketball) "Scott Perry (basketball)") following a five-year run of not making the playoffs. In the seasons leading up to these events, the organization did not have luck in the [NBA draft lottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_draft_lottery "NBA draft lottery") and decided to make more short-sighted trades with the hope to overcome their postseason losing streak.

On May 22, 2017, the Orlando Magic hired Weltman as their new president of basketball operations, and they announced they would give up their less desirable 2018 second-round NBA draft pick to the Raptors as compensation.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-7) Around this time, the Orlando Magic had promising young talent with [Aaron Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Gordon "Aaron Gordon"), [Elfrid Payton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elfrid_Payton_(basketball) "Elfrid Payton (basketball)") and [Nikola Vucevic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Vucevic "Nikola Vucevic"). In the [2017 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_NBA_draft "2017 NBA draft"), the Magic selected [Jonathan Isaac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Isaac "Jonathan Isaac") with the 6th pick.

In May 2018, Orlando added new coach [Steve Clifford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford "Steve Clifford") on a four-year deal.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-8) Weltman said "Steve is widely regarded throughout the NBA community as an elite coach and developer of players at all stages. His teams have always been disciplined and prepared and have embraced the concept of playing for each other.”[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-9) In the [2018 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_NBA_draft "2018 NBA draft"), the Magic selected [Mohamed Bamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Bamba "Mohamed Bamba") with the 6th pick, and [Melvin Frazier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvin_Frazier "Melvin Frazier") with the 35th pick.

Following the [2018–19 Orlando Magic season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_Orlando_Magic_season "2018–19 Orlando Magic season"), Weltman re-signed [Nikola Vucevic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Vucevic "Nikola Vucevic"), [Terrence Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrence_Ross "Terrence Ross") and [Michael Carter-Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Carter-Williams "Michael Carter-Williams") and acquired [Al-Farouq Aminu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Farouq_Aminu "Al-Farouq Aminu"). In the [2019 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_draft "2019 NBA draft"), the Magic selected [Chuma Okeke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuma_Okeke "Chuma Okeke") with the 16th pick. In the [2020 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_NBA_draft "2020 NBA draft"), the Magic selected [Cole Anthony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cole_Anthony "Cole Anthony") with the 15th pick.

In 2021, Weltman said the group was confident that [Markelle Fultz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markelle_Fultz "Markelle Fultz") and [Jonathan Isaac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Isaac "Jonathan Isaac") would fully recover from their injuries but that the current situation was a "toxic brew".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-10) Under Weltman's leadership, the Magic moved [Nikola Vucevic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Vucevic "Nikola Vucevic"), [Evan Fournier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Fournier "Evan Fournier"), and [Aaron Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Gordon "Aaron Gordon") (who requested a trade) in three separate deals at the [2021 trade deadline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_2020%E2%80%9321_NBA_season_transactions "List of 2020–21 NBA season transactions"), acquiring three future first-round picks, [Gary Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Harris "Gary Harris"), an expiring contract in [Otto Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Porter "Otto Porter"), as well as [Wendell Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendell_Carter "Wendell Carter") and [R. J. Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hampton "R. J. Hampton").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-13) With the absence of those veteran players, young talent such as [Mohamed Bamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Bamba "Mohamed Bamba"), [Chuma Okeke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuma_Okeke "Chuma Okeke") and [Dwayne Bacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwayne_Bacon "Dwayne Bacon") would be given more minutes to showcase their skills.

Weltman said "Anytime you trade a player like [Nikola Vucevic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Vucevic "Nikola Vucevic"), it is a tough decision to make...Vooch' will go down as one of the best players to ever wear a Magic uniform".

**Jeff Weltman** is an American [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") executive who is the president of basketball operations for the Orlando Magic of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA).[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-1)

In 2020, Weltman received one 1st place vote for [NBA Executive of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_Executive_of_the_Year "NBA Executive of the Year").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-3)

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeff_Weltman&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Weltman grew up in [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"). He was raised by his father, [Harry Weltman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Weltman "Harry Weltman"), and his mother, Arlene. Harry Weltman was a former GM for the now defunct [ABA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Basketball_Association "American Basketball Association")'s [Spirits of St. Louis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spirits_of_St._Louis "Spirits of St. Louis") in the mid-1970s and for the [Cleveland Cavaliers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Cavaliers "Cleveland Cavaliers") and [New Jersey Nets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Nets "New Jersey Nets") in the mid-1980s. As a teenager, Weltman played pick-up basketball in the [South Bronx](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Bronx "South Bronx") and [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem") on Saturdays. Weltman played basketball at [Oberlin College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberlin_College "Oberlin College") in Ohio.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-4)

At the start of Weltman's career, he was hired by the Clippers as a video coordinator in the late 1990s. Weltman then served as the director of player personnel with the [Los Angeles Clippers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Clippers "Los Angeles Clippers"), director of basketball administration with the [Detroit Pistons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit_Pistons "Detroit Pistons"), assistant GM with the [Denver Nuggets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver_Nuggets "Denver Nuggets") and [Milwaukee Bucks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milwaukee_Bucks "Milwaukee Bucks") and EVP of basketball operations and GM with the [Toronto Raptors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto_Raptors "Toronto Raptors").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-6) Before Weltman joined the Raptors, the Raptors were on a five-year playoff-drought. During Weltman's four-year tenure with the Raptors, the team qualified for the postseason every season and won three playoff series. He then was offered the job of President of Basketball Operations for the Orlando Magic. He took the position and moved to Orlando with his wife, Alexis, and his twin daughters, JJ and Lucy.

## Orlando Magic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jeff_Weltman&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Orlando Magic")]

On April 13, 2017, the Magic fired GM [Rob Hennigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rob_Hennigan "Rob Hennigan") and assistant GM [Scott Perry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_Perry_(basketball) "Scott Perry (basketball)") following a five-year run of not making the playoffs. In the seasons leading up to these events, the organization did not have luck in the [NBA draft lottery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_draft_lottery "NBA draft lottery") and decided to make more short-sighted trades with the hope to overcome their postseason losing streak.

On May 22, 2017, the Orlando Magic hired Weltman as their new president of basketball operations, and they announced they would give up their less desirable 2018 second-round NBA draft pick to the Raptors as compensation.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-7) Around this time, the Orlando Magic had promising young talent with [Aaron Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Gordon "Aaron Gordon"), [Elfrid Payton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elfrid_Payton_(basketball) "Elfrid Payton (basketball)") and [Nikola Vucevic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Vucevic "Nikola Vucevic"). In the [2017 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_NBA_draft "2017 NBA draft"), the Magic selected [Jonathan Isaac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Isaac "Jonathan Isaac") with the 6th pick.

In May 2018, Orlando added new coach [Steve Clifford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford "Steve Clifford") on a four-year deal.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-8) Weltman said "Steve is widely regarded throughout the NBA community as an elite coach and developer of players at all stages. His teams have always been disciplined and prepared and have embraced the concept of playing for each other.”[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-9) In the [2018 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_NBA_draft "2018 NBA draft"), the Magic selected [Mohamed Bamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Bamba "Mohamed Bamba") with the 6th pick, and [Melvin Frazier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melvin_Frazier "Melvin Frazier") with the 35th pick.

Following the [2018–19 Orlando Magic season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018%E2%80%9319_Orlando_Magic_season "2018–19 Orlando Magic season"), Weltman re-signed [Nikola Vucevic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Vucevic "Nikola Vucevic"), [Terrence Ross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terrence_Ross "Terrence Ross") and [Michael Carter-Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Carter-Williams "Michael Carter-Williams") and acquired [Al-Farouq Aminu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Farouq_Aminu "Al-Farouq Aminu"). In the [2019 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_NBA_draft "2019 NBA draft"), the Magic selected [Chuma Okeke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuma_Okeke "Chuma Okeke") with the 16th pick. In the [2020 NBA draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_NBA_draft "2020 NBA draft"), the Magic selected [Cole Anthony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cole_Anthony "Cole Anthony") with the 15th pick.

In 2021, Weltman said the group was confident that [Markelle Fultz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markelle_Fultz "Markelle Fultz") and [Jonathan Isaac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Isaac "Jonathan Isaac") would fully recover from their injuries but that the current situation was a "toxic brew".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-10) Under Weltman's leadership, the Magic moved [Nikola Vucevic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Vucevic "Nikola Vucevic"), [Evan Fournier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evan_Fournier "Evan Fournier"), and [Aaron Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aaron_Gordon "Aaron Gordon") (who requested a trade) in three separate deals at the [2021 trade deadline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_2020%E2%80%9321_NBA_season_transactions "List of 2020–21 NBA season transactions"), acquiring three future first-round picks, [Gary Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Harris "Gary Harris"), an expiring contract in [Otto Porter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Otto_Porter "Otto Porter"), as well as [Wendell Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendell_Carter "Wendell Carter") and [R. J. Hampton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R._J._Hampton "R. J. Hampton").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Weltman#cite_note-13) With the absence of those veteran players, young talent such as [Mohamed Bamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohamed_Bamba "Mohamed Bamba"), [Chuma Okeke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuma_Okeke "Chuma Okeke") and [Dwayne Bacon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwayne_Bacon "Dwayne Bacon") would be given more minutes to showcase their skills.

Weltman said "Anytime you trade a player like [Nikola Vucevic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikola_Vucevic "Nikola Vucevic"), it is a tough decision to make...Vooch' will go down as one of the best players to ever wear a Magic uniform".

**Stephanie Diana Wilson** (born September 27, 1966)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-womenastronauts-1) is an American [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer") and a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). She flew to space onboard three [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") missions and is the second [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American "African American") woman to go into space after [Mae Jemison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mae_Jemison "Mae Jemison"). As of 2026,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit) her almost 43 days in space are the second most of any female African American astronaut, having been surpassed by [Jessica Watkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Watkins "Jessica Watkins") in 2022.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Wilson was born in [Boston, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Massachusetts "Boston, Massachusetts") on September 27, 1966. About a year later, her parents, Eugene and Barbara Wilson,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2) decided to move to [Pittsfield, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsfield,_Massachusetts "Pittsfield, Massachusetts").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-3) Eugene, a native of [Nesmith, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesmith,_South_Carolina "Nesmith, South Carolina"), used his electronics training from his time in the Navy to get himself a degree from [Northeastern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_University "Northeastern University") and a long career in electrical engineering for [Raytheon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raytheon "Raytheon"), [Sprague Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_C._Sprague "Robert C. Sprague"), and [Lockheed Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-4) while Barbara, from [Talbot County, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_County,_Georgia "Talbot County, Georgia"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-5) worked as a production assistant for Lockheed Martin.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2)

After attending Stearns Elementary School, she attended Crosby Junior High School.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-iberkshires.com-6) For a career awareness class in middle school, Wilson was assigned to interview someone in a field that interested her. Since she liked to look up at the sky,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-7) she interviewed [Williams College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williams_College "Williams College") astronomer [Jay Pasachoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Pasachoff "Jay Pasachoff"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-iberkshires.com-6) clarifying her potential career interest in space. In high school, Eugene encouraged Stephanie to go into engineering,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2) so she decided to become an aerospace engineer.

Wilson graduated from Taconic High School, Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in 1984. She attended [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), receiving a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in engineering science in 1988. Wilson earned a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in aerospace engineering from the [University of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") in 1992.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-womenastronauts-1) Wilson has returned to Harvard as a member of the [Harvard Board of Overseers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Board_of_Overseers "Harvard Board of Overseers").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-8) She was the Chief Marshal for the 362nd Harvard Commencement on May 30, 2013.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-9)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Engineering

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Engineering")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg/250px-STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg)

Wilson during STS-120, with a model of Node 2 "STS-120") floating in front of her

Wilson worked for two years for the former [Martin Marietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Marietta "Martin Marietta") Astronautics Group in Denver, Colorado. As a Loads and Dynamics engineer for the [Titan IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_IV "Titan IV") rocket, Wilson was responsible for performing coupled loads analyses for the launch vehicle and payloads during flight events. Wilson left Martin Marietta in 1990 to attend graduate school at the University of Texas. Her research focused on the control and modeling of large, flexible space structures.

Following the completion of her graduate work, Wilson began working for the [Jet Propulsion Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Propulsion_Laboratory "Jet Propulsion Laboratory") in [Pasadena, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena,_California "Pasadena, California"), in 1992. As a member of the Attitude and Articulation Control Subsystem for the [Galileo spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_spacecraft "Galileo spacecraft"), Wilson was responsible for assessing attitude controller performance, science platform pointing accuracy, antenna pointing accuracy, and spin rate accuracy. She worked in the areas of sequence development and testing as well. While at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Wilson also supported the Interferometery Technology Program as a member of the Integrated Modeling Team, which was responsible for finite element modeling, controller design, and software development.

## NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NASA")]

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") as an astronaut candidate in April 1996, Wilson reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1996. Having completed two years of training and evaluation, she is qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. She was initially assigned technical duties in the Astronaut Office Space Station Operations Branch to work with Space Station payload displays and procedures. She then served in the Astronaut Office [CAPCOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller#Spacecraft_communicator_(CAPCOM) "Flight controller") Branch, working in Mission Control as a prime communicator with on-orbit crews. Following her work in Mission Control, Wilson was assigned technical duties in the Astronaut Office Shuttle Operations Branch involving the Space Shuttle Main Engines, External Tank and Solid Rocket Boosters.

Wilson has flown on three shuttle missions. On [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121"), Wilson flew aboard as a mission specialist. She also flew on the STS-120 mission that delivered the [Harmony connecting module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony_Module "Harmony Module") to the International Space Station.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-NASAbio-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-12) In April 2010, Wilson flew as a mission specialist on [STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131").

On October 18, 2019, Wilson was ground controller at [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") for the first all woman spacewalk by [Christina Koch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Koch "Christina Koch") and [Jessica Meir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Meir "Jessica Meir").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-13)

On December 9, 2020, NASA announced that Stephanie Wilson was among the candidates for the [Artemis program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program"), and if selected, she could be both the first woman and the first African-American on the Moon.

On January 31, 2024, NASA announced that Wilson would fly as mission specialist on the [SpaceX Crew-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Crew-9 "SpaceX Crew-9") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-14) However, when NASA decided to return the [Boeing Starliner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Starliner "Boeing Starliner") capsule on the [Boeing Crew Flight Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Crew_Flight_Test "Boeing Crew Flight Test") uncrewed, Wilson was removed from Crew-9, along with commander and fellow astronaut [Zena Cardman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zena_Cardman "Zena Cardman"), to make room on the return journey for the Starliner astronauts, [Barry E. Wilmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_E._Wilmore "Barry E. Wilmore") and [Sunita Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunita_Williams "Sunita Williams").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-15) On September 28, 2024, she made a brief appearance during NASA's coverage of the Crew-9 launch, which was co-hosted by Cardman and NASA communicator Derrol Nail. Cardman had commented during the nearly five-hour broadcast at length on the experience that [Nick Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Hague "Nick Hague") and [Roscosmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscosmos "Roscosmos") cosmonaut [Aleksandr Gorbunov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Gorbunov "Aleksandr Gorbunov") were going through as they successfully launched from [Cape Canaveral Space Force Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Canaveral_Space_Force_Station "Cape Canaveral Space Force Station") in Florida.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-16)

### Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

#### STS-121

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: STS-121")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg/250px-Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg)

Wilson participates in a training session in the Space Vehicle Mock-up Facility at NASA's [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center")

[STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") (July 4–17, 2006), was a return-to-flight test mission and assembly flight to the International Space Station. During the 13-day flight, the crew of Space Shuttle Discovery tested new equipment and procedures that increase the safety of space shuttles, repaired a rail car on the International Space Station and produced never-before-seen, high-resolution images of the Shuttle during and after its July 4 launch. Wilson supported robotic arm operations for vehicle inspection, [Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module") installation and EVAs and was responsible for transferring more than 28,000 pounds of supplies and equipment to the ISS. The crew also performed maintenance on the space station and delivered a new [Expedition 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_13 "Expedition 13") crew member to the station. The mission was accomplished in 306 hours, 37 minutes, and 54 seconds.

#### STS-120

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: STS-120")]

STS-120 (October 23 – November 7, 2007) was a 6.25 million mile [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission to the International Space Station.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-main-17) It delivered the _[Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony\_Module "Harmony Module")_ module, and reconfigured the [P6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure#P6,_S6_trusses "Integrated Truss Structure") truss in preparation for future assembly missions.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-presskit-18) STS-120 carried a new [Expedition 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_16 "Expedition 16") crew member, [Daniel Tani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Tani "Daniel Tani"), and returned [Expedition 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_15 "Expedition 15") and Expedition 16 crewmember [Clayton Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson "Clayton Anderson"). The crew conducted four [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") and performed a previously untested repair method on the station's solar array. The mission was accomplished in 15 days, 2 hours, 23 minutes, during 238 orbits.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-finalsr-19)

#### STS-131

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: STS-131")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg/330px-STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg)

The four astronauts of [STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131") and [Expedition 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_23 "Expedition 23") (Wilson to the bottom right), the first time four women being at the same time in space.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-20)

[STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131") (April 5–20, 2010) was a resupply mission to the International Space Station. Space Shuttle Discovery was launched pre-dawn from Kennedy Space Center. Once docked to the space station, the crew delivered more than 27,000 pounds of hardware, supplies, experiments and equipment, including a tank full of ammonia coolant that required three spacewalks and robotics to install, new crew sleeping quarters, a window observation facility and a freezer for experiments.

During the mission, Wilson was responsible for robotics for spacewalking support using the space station robotic arm and for robotic removal of the "Leonardo" Multi-Purpose Logistics Module from the payload bay of Discovery. For the return to Earth, Wilson robotically installed Leonardo, which was packed with more than 6,000 pounds of hardware, science results and used supplies, inside Discovery's payload bay. The STS-131 mission was accomplished in 15 days, 2 hours, 47 minutes, and 10 seconds and traveled 6,232,235 statute miles in 238 orbits.

#### Artemis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Artemis")]

[Artemis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program") (2017–present) is the mission NASA announced in 2020 to return to the Moon.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-21) Wilson has been selected as one of 18 astronauts comprising the Artemis team.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-23)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Wilson is a Christian.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-24) She is a member of [Alpha Kappa Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Kappa_Alpha "Alpha Kappa Alpha") sorority.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-25) Her hobbies include skiing and stamp collecting.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-26) She married Julius "BJ" McCurdy, a television producer, in June 1999.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-30) The couple divorced in 2003.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-31)

## Awards and honors

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Awards and honors")]

*   [NASA Distinguished Service Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Distinguished_Service_Medal "NASA Distinguished Service Medal") (2009, 2011)
*   [NASA Space Flight Medal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Space_Flight_Medal "NASA Space Flight Medal") (2006, 2007, 2010)
*   Honorary Doctorate of Science from Williams College (2011)
*   Harvard College Women's Professional Achievement Award (2008)
*   Harvard Foundation Scientist of the Year Award (2008)
*   Young Outstanding Texas Exes Award (2005)
*   Johnson Space Center Innovation Group Achievement Award (2013)
*   Johnson Space Center Director Commendation Award (2013)
*   Salem Trailblazer Award (2019)
