**Stephanie Diana Wilson** (born September 27, 1966)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-womenastronauts-1) is an American [engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineer "Engineer") and a [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). She flew to space onboard three [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") missions and is the second [African American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_American "African American") woman to go into space after [Mae Jemison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mae_Jemison "Mae Jemison"). As of 2026,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit) her almost 43 days in space are the second most of any female African American astronaut, having been surpassed by [Jessica Watkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Watkins "Jessica Watkins") in 2022.

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Wilson was born in [Boston, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston,_Massachusetts "Boston, Massachusetts") on September 27, 1966. About a year later, her parents, Eugene and Barbara Wilson,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2) decided to move to [Pittsfield, Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsfield,_Massachusetts "Pittsfield, Massachusetts").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-3) Eugene, a native of [Nesmith, South Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nesmith,_South_Carolina "Nesmith, South Carolina"), used his electronics training from his time in the Navy to get himself a degree from [Northeastern University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeastern_University "Northeastern University") and a long career in electrical engineering for [Raytheon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raytheon "Raytheon"), [Sprague Electric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_C._Sprague "Robert C. Sprague"), and [Lockheed Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin "Lockheed Martin"),[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-4) while Barbara, from [Talbot County, Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talbot_County,_Georgia "Talbot County, Georgia"),[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-5) worked as a production assistant for Lockheed Martin.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2)

After attending Stearns Elementary School, she attended Crosby Junior High School.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-iberkshires.com-6) For a career awareness class in middle school, Wilson was assigned to interview someone in a field that interested her. Since she liked to look up at the sky,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-7) she interviewed [Williams College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Williams_College "Williams College") astronomer [Jay Pasachoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Pasachoff "Jay Pasachoff"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-iberkshires.com-6) clarifying her potential career interest in space. In high school, Eugene encouraged Stephanie to go into engineering,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-:0-2) so she decided to become an aerospace engineer.

Wilson graduated from Taconic High School, Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in 1984. She attended [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"), receiving a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in engineering science in 1988. Wilson earned a [Master of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Science "Master of Science") degree in aerospace engineering from the [University of Texas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Texas_at_Austin "University of Texas at Austin") in 1992.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-womenastronauts-1) Wilson has returned to Harvard as a member of the [Harvard Board of Overseers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Board_of_Overseers "Harvard Board of Overseers").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-8) She was the Chief Marshal for the 362nd Harvard Commencement on May 30, 2013.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-9)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Engineering

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Engineering")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2c/STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg/250px-STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS120_Day_7_Harmony_Model.jpg)

Wilson during STS-120, with a model of Node 2 "STS-120") floating in front of her

Wilson worked for two years for the former [Martin Marietta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Marietta "Martin Marietta") Astronautics Group in Denver, Colorado. As a Loads and Dynamics engineer for the [Titan IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titan_IV "Titan IV") rocket, Wilson was responsible for performing coupled loads analyses for the launch vehicle and payloads during flight events. Wilson left Martin Marietta in 1990 to attend graduate school at the University of Texas. Her research focused on the control and modeling of large, flexible space structures.

Following the completion of her graduate work, Wilson began working for the [Jet Propulsion Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_Propulsion_Laboratory "Jet Propulsion Laboratory") in [Pasadena, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pasadena,_California "Pasadena, California"), in 1992. As a member of the Attitude and Articulation Control Subsystem for the [Galileo spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galileo_spacecraft "Galileo spacecraft"), Wilson was responsible for assessing attitude controller performance, science platform pointing accuracy, antenna pointing accuracy, and spin rate accuracy. She worked in the areas of sequence development and testing as well. While at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Wilson also supported the Interferometery Technology Program as a member of the Integrated Modeling Team, which was responsible for finite element modeling, controller design, and software development.

## NASA

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: NASA")]

Selected by [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA") as an astronaut candidate in April 1996, Wilson reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1996. Having completed two years of training and evaluation, she is qualified for flight assignment as a mission specialist. She was initially assigned technical duties in the Astronaut Office Space Station Operations Branch to work with Space Station payload displays and procedures. She then served in the Astronaut Office [CAPCOM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_controller#Spacecraft_communicator_(CAPCOM) "Flight controller") Branch, working in Mission Control as a prime communicator with on-orbit crews. Following her work in Mission Control, Wilson was assigned technical duties in the Astronaut Office Shuttle Operations Branch involving the Space Shuttle Main Engines, External Tank and Solid Rocket Boosters.

Wilson has flown on three shuttle missions. On [STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121"), Wilson flew aboard as a mission specialist. She also flew on the STS-120 mission that delivered the [Harmony connecting module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony_Module "Harmony Module") to the International Space Station.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-NASAbio-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-12) In April 2010, Wilson flew as a mission specialist on [STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131").

On October 18, 2019, Wilson was ground controller at [Houston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") for the first all woman spacewalk by [Christina Koch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christina_Koch "Christina Koch") and [Jessica Meir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jessica_Meir "Jessica Meir").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-13)

On December 9, 2020, NASA announced that Stephanie Wilson was among the candidates for the [Artemis program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program"), and if selected, she could be both the first woman and the first African-American on the Moon.

On January 31, 2024, NASA announced that Wilson would fly as mission specialist on the [SpaceX Crew-9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SpaceX_Crew-9 "SpaceX Crew-9") mission to the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-14) However, when NASA decided to return the [Boeing Starliner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Starliner "Boeing Starliner") capsule on the [Boeing Crew Flight Test](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_Crew_Flight_Test "Boeing Crew Flight Test") uncrewed, Wilson was removed from Crew-9, along with commander and fellow astronaut [Zena Cardman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zena_Cardman "Zena Cardman"), to make room on the return journey for the Starliner astronauts, [Barry E. Wilmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_E._Wilmore "Barry E. Wilmore") and [Sunita Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunita_Williams "Sunita Williams").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-15) On September 28, 2024, she made a brief appearance during NASA's coverage of the Crew-9 launch, which was co-hosted by Cardman and NASA communicator Derrol Nail. Cardman had commented during the nearly five-hour broadcast at length on the experience that [Nick Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Hague "Nick Hague") and [Roscosmos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roscosmos "Roscosmos") cosmonaut [Aleksandr Gorbunov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aleksandr_Gorbunov "Aleksandr Gorbunov") were going through as they successfully launched from [Cape Canaveral Space Force Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Canaveral_Space_Force_Station "Cape Canaveral Space Force Station") in Florida.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-16)

### Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

#### STS-121

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: STS-121")]

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/18/Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg/250px-Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jsc2009e207942Wilson.jpg)

Wilson participates in a training session in the Space Vehicle Mock-up Facility at NASA's [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center")

[STS-121](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-121 "STS-121") (July 4–17, 2006), was a return-to-flight test mission and assembly flight to the International Space Station. During the 13-day flight, the crew of Space Shuttle Discovery tested new equipment and procedures that increase the safety of space shuttles, repaired a rail car on the International Space Station and produced never-before-seen, high-resolution images of the Shuttle during and after its July 4 launch. Wilson supported robotic arm operations for vehicle inspection, [Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module") installation and EVAs and was responsible for transferring more than 28,000 pounds of supplies and equipment to the ISS. The crew also performed maintenance on the space station and delivered a new [Expedition 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_13 "Expedition 13") crew member to the station. The mission was accomplished in 306 hours, 37 minutes, and 54 seconds.

#### STS-120

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: STS-120")]

STS-120 (October 23 – November 7, 2007) was a 6.25 million mile [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle") mission to the International Space Station.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-main-17) It delivered the _[Harmony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmony\_Module "Harmony Module")_ module, and reconfigured the [P6](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Truss_Structure#P6,_S6_trusses "Integrated Truss Structure") truss in preparation for future assembly missions.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-presskit-18) STS-120 carried a new [Expedition 16](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_16 "Expedition 16") crew member, [Daniel Tani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Tani "Daniel Tani"), and returned [Expedition 15](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_15 "Expedition 15") and Expedition 16 crewmember [Clayton Anderson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clayton_Anderson "Clayton Anderson"). The crew conducted four [spacewalks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") and performed a previously untested repair method on the station's solar array. The mission was accomplished in 15 days, 2 hours, 23 minutes, during 238 orbits.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-finalsr-19)

#### STS-131

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: STS-131")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b2/STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg/330px-STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:STS-131_ISS-23_Four_Astronauts.jpg)

The four astronauts of [STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131") and [Expedition 23](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expedition_23 "Expedition 23") (Wilson to the bottom right), the first time four women being at the same time in space.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-20)

[STS-131](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-131 "STS-131") (April 5–20, 2010) was a resupply mission to the International Space Station. Space Shuttle Discovery was launched pre-dawn from Kennedy Space Center. Once docked to the space station, the crew delivered more than 27,000 pounds of hardware, supplies, experiments and equipment, including a tank full of ammonia coolant that required three spacewalks and robotics to install, new crew sleeping quarters, a window observation facility and a freezer for experiments.

During the mission, Wilson was responsible for robotics for spacewalking support using the space station robotic arm and for robotic removal of the "Leonardo" Multi-Purpose Logistics Module from the payload bay of Discovery. For the return to Earth, Wilson robotically installed Leonardo, which was packed with more than 6,000 pounds of hardware, science results and used supplies, inside Discovery's payload bay. The STS-131 mission was accomplished in 15 days, 2 hours, 47 minutes, and 10 seconds and traveled 6,232,235 statute miles in 238 orbits.

#### Artemis

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Artemis")]

[Artemis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artemis_program "Artemis program") (2017–present) is the mission NASA announced in 2020 to return to the Moon.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-21) Wilson has been selected as one of 18 astronauts comprising the Artemis team.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-23)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Stephanie_Wilson&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Wilson is a Christian.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-24) She is a member of [Alpha Kappa Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Kappa_Alpha "Alpha Kappa Alpha") sorority.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-25) Her hobbies include skiing and stamp collecting.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-26) She married Julius "BJ" McCurdy, a television producer, in June 1999.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-30) The couple divorced in 2003.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Wilson#cite_note-31)

**Scott Edward Parazynski** (born July 28, 1961) is an American physician and former [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). A veteran of five Space Shuttle flights and seven spacewalks, Parazynski's latest mission was STS-120 in October 2007 – highlighted by a dramatic, unplanned [extra-vehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) to repair a live solar array. In May 2016, he was inducted into the [United States Astronaut Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Astronaut_Hall_of_Fame "United States Astronaut Hall of Fame"). He retired from NASA in March 2009 to pursue entrepreneurial opportunities in the private sector, and he is currently the CEO of a technology start-up. He is the first person to have both flown in space and summited [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), the highest point on Earth.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-1) He describes his life's experiences in his 2017 memoir _The Sky Below_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-2)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Parazynski is of [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people "Polish people") descent, as his great-great-grandparents migrated from [Kraków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krak%C3%B3w "Kraków") to the US.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-se-3) He considers [Palo Alto, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto,_California "Palo Alto, California"), and [Evergreen, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evergreen,_Colorado "Evergreen, Colorado"), to be his hometowns. He is married to [Meenakshi Wadhwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meenakshi_Wadhwa "Meenakshi Wadhwa"), a planetary scientist at Arizona State University. He has two children with his first wife, Gail. Scott enjoys [mountaineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering"), [rock climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_climbing "Rock climbing"), [flying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly "Fly") and [scuba diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_diving "Scuba diving"). A commercial, multi-engine, seaplane and instrument-rated [pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviator "Aviator"), Parazynski has logged over 2500 flight hours in a variety of aircraft. As a mountaineer, his [summits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographical_summit "Topographical summit") include [Cerro Aconcagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Aconcagua "Cerro Aconcagua") (at 22,841 feet (6,962 m) above sea level, the tallest [mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") in the world outside [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia")) and all 59 of [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado")'s peaks over 14,000 feet (4,300 m) in [altitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude "Altitude"). He first attempted to summit [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") in May 2008, but was forced to turn back before the summit due to a severe back injury. Serving as team physician for the Discovery Channel[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-4) a year later, at 4:00 am on May 20, 2009, he successfully summited the 29,029 feet (8,848 m) mountain.

Other notable expeditions include a scientific dive into the summit caldera lake atop [Licancabur Volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licancabur "Licancabur") (19,409 feet (5,916 m) on the Bolivian-Chilean border), one of the world's highest lakes, and setting the first bootprints adjacent Masaya Volcano's lava lake in Nicaragua with Sam Cossman in 2016.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-5) He also travelled aboard [OceanGate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OceanGate "OceanGate")'s submersible _Titan_ and visited the [wreck of the _Titanic_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreck_of_the_Titanic "Wreck of the Titanic") in the North Atlantic.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-7)

## Education and early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education and early life")]

Parazynski attended junior high school at Dakar Academy in [Dakar, Senegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar,_Senegal "Dakar, Senegal"), and [Beirut, Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beirut,_Lebanon "Beirut, Lebanon"). In March 1969 as an eight-year-old, he travelled to Florida to witness the launch of [Apollo 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_9 "Apollo 9"), an event he argued inspired him to pursue a career in science. He attended high school at the [Community School, Tehran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_School,_Tehran "Community School, Tehran"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), and the [American Community School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Community_Schools "American Community Schools"), [Athens, Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens,_Greece "Athens, Greece"), graduating in 1979. He received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology") from [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") in 1983, continuing on to graduate with honors from [Stanford Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Medical_School "Stanford Medical School") in 1989. He served his medical internship at the [Brigham and Women's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_and_Women's_Hospital "Brigham and Women's Hospital") of [Harvard Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Medical_School "Harvard Medical School") (1990). He had completed 22 months of a residency program in emergency medicine in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"), [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado"), when selected for the NASA Astronaut Corps.

## Organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Organizations")]

Parazynski is a Fellow of the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association") and [The Explorers Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Explorers_Club "The Explorers Club"). Additionally, he is a member of the American Society for Gravitational and Space Biology, the [Wilderness Medical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilderness_Medical_Society "Wilderness Medical Society"), the [American Alpine Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Alpine_Club "American Alpine Club"), the [Association of Space Explorers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Space_Explorers "Association of Space Explorers"), the [Experimental Aircraft Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_Aircraft_Association "Experimental Aircraft Association"), and the [Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_Owners_and_Pilots_Association "Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association"). He is president of the board of directors of the [Challenger Center for Space Science Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Center_for_Space_Science_Education "Challenger Center for Space Science Education"), and serves on the boards of the [Houston Museum of Natural Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Museum_of_Natural_Science "Houston Museum of Natural Science"), the University of Texas McDonald Observatory and [OceanGate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OceanGate "OceanGate").

In 2014, Parazynski was appointed as a professor of practice at [Arizona State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_State_University "Arizona State University"), and was designated ASU's first University Explorer.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-8) He subsequently founded Fluidity Technologies[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-9) based on his intellectual property, a company aiming to manufacture and distribute novel control devices for mobility in 3-D space, for everything from drones and computer games to VR and surgical robotics.

## Medical career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Medical career")]

While an [undergraduate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate "Undergraduate") at [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"), Parazynski studied [antigenic shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigenic_shift "Antigenic shift") in [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa")[sleeping sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_trypanosomiasis "African trypanosomiasis"), using sophisticated [molecular biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_biology "Molecular biology") techniques. During [medical school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_school "Medical school"), he was awarded a NASA graduate student [fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarship "Scholarship") and conducted [research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research "Research") at [NASA Ames Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Ames_Research_Center "NASA Ames Research Center") on [fluid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid "Fluid") shifts that occur during human [space flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_flight "Space flight"). Additionally, he has been involved in the design of several [exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exercise "Exercise") devices that are being developed for long-duration [space flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_flight "Space flight"), and has conducted research on high-[altitude acclimatization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude_acclimatization "Altitude acclimatization"). Parazynski has numerous publications in the field of space [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology"), and has a particular expertise in human [adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptation_(biology) "Adaptation (biology)") to stressful environments.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected as an astronaut in March 1992, Parazynski reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1992. He completed one year of training and evaluation, and was qualified as a mission specialist. Parazynski initially served as one of the crew representatives for [extra-vehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) in the Astronaut Office Mission Development Branch. Following his first flight, he was assigned as a backup for the third American long-duration stay aboard Russia's [space station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station")[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir"), and was expected to serve as a prime crew member on a subsequent mission. He spent five months in training at the [Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gagarin_Cosmonaut_Training_Center "Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center"), [Star City, Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City,_Moscow "Star City, Moscow"), Russia.

In October 1995, when sitting-height parameters raised concerns about his fitting safely in the [Soyuz spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_spacecraft "Soyuz spacecraft") in the event of an emergency on board the Mir station, he was deemed too tall for the mission and was withdrawn from Mir training. He has served as the Astronaut Office Operations Planning Branch crew representative for [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle"), Space Station and Soyuz training, and also served as Deputy (Operations and Training) of the Astronaut Office [ISS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") Branch. Most recently, he served as Chief of the Astronaut Office EVA Branch. A veteran of five space flights, [STS-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-66 "STS-66") (1994), [STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86") (1997), [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") (1998), [STS-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-100 "STS-100") (2001), and STS-120 (2007), Parazynski has logged over 1,019 hours (8 weeks) in space, including 47 hours of EVA, and traveled over 17 million miles. Parazynski's most recent mission was STS-120, during which he performed four spacewalks to continue International Space Station assembly. The fourth EVA is considered one of the most challenging and dangerous ever performed: while perched on the end of a 90-foot robotic boom, further away from the safety of the airlock than anyone had previously ventured, he had to repair a fully energized solar array. He became only the second NASA astronaut to perform four spacewalks during a single shuttle mission. A photo that he took during one of the spacewalks was listed on _[Popular Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular\_Science "Popular Science")_'s photo gallery of the best [astronaut selfies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_selfie "Astronaut selfie").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-21)

## Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg/250px-Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg)

Scott Parazynski during a spacewalk during STS-120.

The [STS-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-66 "STS-66") Atmospheric [Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laboratory "Laboratory") for Applications and Science-3 (ATLAS-3) mission was launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on November 3, 1994, and returned to land at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on November 14, 1994. ATLAS-3 was part of an ongoing program to determine the Earth's [energy balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_energy_budget#Earth's_energy_imbalance_(EEI) "Earth's energy budget") and [atmospheric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere") change over an 11-year [solar cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cycle "Solar cycle"), particularly with respect to humanity's impact on global-[ozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone "Ozone") distribution. Parazynski had responsibility for a number of on-orbit activities including operation of the ATLAS experiments and [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") Pallet, as well as several secondary experiments in the crew cabin. He and his crewmates also successfully evaluated the Interlimb Resistance Device, a free-floating exercise he developed to prevent [muscular atrophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscular_atrophy "Muscular atrophy") in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microgravity "Microgravity"). [Space Shuttle _Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis") circled the earth 175 times and traveled over 4.5 million miles during its 262-hour and 34-minute flight.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

[STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86")_Atlantis_ (September 25 to October 6, 1997) was the seventh mission to rendezvous and dock with the Russian Space Station Mir. Highlights of the mission included the exchange of U.S. crew members [Michael Foale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Foale "Michael Foale") and [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"), the transfer of 10,400 pounds of science and logistics, and the first Shuttle-based joint American-Russian spacewalk. Parazynski served as the flight engineer (MS2) during the flight, and was also the navigator during the Mir rendezvous. Parazynski (EV1) and Russian [cosmonaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmonaut "Cosmonaut")[Vladimir Titov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Titov_(cosmonaut) "Vladimir Titov (cosmonaut)") performed a 5-hour, 1 minute [spacewalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalk "Spacewalk") during which they retrieved four experiment packages first deployed during the [STS-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-76 "STS-76")[Shuttle-Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle-Mir "Shuttle-Mir") docking mission. They also deployed the Spektr Solar Array Cap, which was designed to be used in a future Mir spacewalk to seal a leak in the Spektr module's damaged hull. Other objectives of EVA included the evaluation of common EVA tools to be used by astronauts wearing either Russian or American-made spacesuits, and a systems flight test of the Simplified Aid for EVA Rescue (SAFER). Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ circled the Earth 169 times and traveled over 4.2 million miles during its 259-hour and 21-minute flight, landing at the Kennedy Space Center.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg/250px-Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg)

 Scott Parazynski during an STS-120 spacewalk to repair a damaged [solar panel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_panel "Solar panel") of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

[STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95")_[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_ (October 29 to November 7, 1998) was a nine-day mission during which the crew supported a variety of research payloads, including deployment of the Spartan solar-observing spacecraft and the testing of the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") Orbital Systems Test Platform. The crew also conducted investigations on the correlation between space flight and the aging process. Parazynski was the flight engineer (MS2) for the mission, as well as the navigator for the Spartan spacecraft rendezvous. During the flight, he also operated the Shuttle's robotic arm in support of the testing of several space-vision systems being considered for ISS assembly. In addition, he was responsible for monitoring several life sciences investigations, including those involving crewmate [Senator John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"). The mission was accomplished in 134 Earth orbits, traveling 3.6 million miles in 213 hours and 44 minutes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

[STS-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-100 "STS-100")_[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (April 19 to May 1, 2001) was the 9th mission to the International Space Station (ISS) Alpha during which the crew successfully delivered and installed the Space Station "Canadarm2" robotic arm, to be used for all future Space Station assembly and maintenance tasks. Parazynski conducted two spacewalks with [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians "Canadians") colleague [Chris Hadfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hadfield "Chris Hadfield") to assemble and power the next generation robotic arm. Additionally, the pair installed a new [UHF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UHF "UHF")[radio antenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_antenna "Radio antenna") for space-to-space communications during Space Shuttle rendezvous and ISS extravehicular activity. A critical on-orbit spare, a [direct current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_current "Direct current") switching unit, was also transferred to Alpha during the 14 hours and 50 minutes of EVA work. Also during the flight, Parazynski operated _Endeavour_'s robotic arm to attach, and later detach, the Italian-built _Raffaello_[Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module"). Traveling 4.9 million miles in 283 hours and 30 minutes, the mission was accomplished in 186 Earth orbits.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

STS-120_Discovery_ (October 23 – November 7, 2007) launched from and returned to land at the Kennedy Space Center, Florida. During the mission, the Node 2 module named _Harmony_ was delivered to the International Space Station. This element opened up the capability for future international laboratories to be added to the station. Parazynski served as EV1 (lead spacewalker) and accumulated over 27 EVA hours in 4 spacewalks. One of the major EVA mission objectives was the relocation of the P6 Solar Array from the top of the Z1 Truss to the end of the port side of the Integrated Truss Structure. During the IVA-commanded re-deploy of the solar array, several array panels snagged and were damaged, requiring an unplanned spacewalk to successfully repair the array. The mission was accomplished in 238 Earth orbits, traveling 6.2 million miles in 15 days, 2 hours, and 23 minutes.

**Scott Edward Parazynski** (born July 28, 1961) is an American physician and former [NASA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA "NASA")[astronaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut "Astronaut"). A veteran of five Space Shuttle flights and seven spacewalks, Parazynski's latest mission was STS-120 in October 2007 – highlighted by a dramatic, unplanned [extra-vehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) to repair a live solar array. In May 2016, he was inducted into the [United States Astronaut Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Astronaut_Hall_of_Fame "United States Astronaut Hall of Fame"). He retired from NASA in March 2009 to pursue entrepreneurial opportunities in the private sector, and he is currently the CEO of a technology start-up. He is the first person to have both flown in space and summited [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest"), the highest point on Earth.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-1) He describes his life's experiences in his 2017 memoir _The Sky Below_.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-2)

## Personal life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Parazynski is of [Polish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polish_people "Polish people") descent, as his great-great-grandparents migrated from [Kraków](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krak%C3%B3w "Kraków") to the US.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-se-3) He considers [Palo Alto, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palo_Alto,_California "Palo Alto, California"), and [Evergreen, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evergreen,_Colorado "Evergreen, Colorado"), to be his hometowns. He is married to [Meenakshi Wadhwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meenakshi_Wadhwa "Meenakshi Wadhwa"), a planetary scientist at Arizona State University. He has two children with his first wife, Gail. Scott enjoys [mountaineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountaineering "Mountaineering"), [rock climbing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rock_climbing "Rock climbing"), [flying](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fly "Fly") and [scuba diving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scuba_diving "Scuba diving"). A commercial, multi-engine, seaplane and instrument-rated [pilot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aviator "Aviator"), Parazynski has logged over 2500 flight hours in a variety of aircraft. As a mountaineer, his [summits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topographical_summit "Topographical summit") include [Cerro Aconcagua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cerro_Aconcagua "Cerro Aconcagua") (at 22,841 feet (6,962 m) above sea level, the tallest [mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain "Mountain") in the world outside [Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asia "Asia")) and all 59 of [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado")'s peaks over 14,000 feet (4,300 m) in [altitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude "Altitude"). He first attempted to summit [Mount Everest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Everest "Mount Everest") in May 2008, but was forced to turn back before the summit due to a severe back injury. Serving as team physician for the Discovery Channel[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-4) a year later, at 4:00 am on May 20, 2009, he successfully summited the 29,029 feet (8,848 m) mountain.

Other notable expeditions include a scientific dive into the summit caldera lake atop [Licancabur Volcano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Licancabur "Licancabur") (19,409 feet (5,916 m) on the Bolivian-Chilean border), one of the world's highest lakes, and setting the first bootprints adjacent Masaya Volcano's lava lake in Nicaragua with Sam Cossman in 2016.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-5) He also travelled aboard [OceanGate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OceanGate "OceanGate")'s submersible _Titan_ and visited the [wreck of the _Titanic_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wreck_of_the_Titanic "Wreck of the Titanic") in the North Atlantic.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-7)

## Education and early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Education and early life")]

Parazynski attended junior high school at Dakar Academy in [Dakar, Senegal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar,_Senegal "Dakar, Senegal"), and [Beirut, Lebanon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beirut,_Lebanon "Beirut, Lebanon"). In March 1969 as an eight-year-old, he travelled to Florida to witness the launch of [Apollo 9](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo_9 "Apollo 9"), an event he argued inspired him to pursue a career in science. He attended high school at the [Community School, Tehran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_School,_Tehran "Community School, Tehran"), [Iran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iran "Iran"), and the [American Community School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Community_Schools "American Community Schools"), [Athens, Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens,_Greece "Athens, Greece"), graduating in 1979. He received a [Bachelor of Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science "Bachelor of Science") degree in [biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biology "Biology") from [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University") in 1983, continuing on to graduate with honors from [Stanford Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_Medical_School "Stanford Medical School") in 1989. He served his medical internship at the [Brigham and Women's Hospital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigham_and_Women's_Hospital "Brigham and Women's Hospital") of [Harvard Medical School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_Medical_School "Harvard Medical School") (1990). He had completed 22 months of a residency program in emergency medicine in [Denver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver "Denver"), [Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado "Colorado"), when selected for the NASA Astronaut Corps.

## Organizations

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Organizations")]

Parazynski is a Fellow of the [Aerospace Medical Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerospace_Medical_Association "Aerospace Medical Association") and [The Explorers Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Explorers_Club "The Explorers Club"). Additionally, he is a member of the American Society for Gravitational and Space Biology, the [Wilderness Medical Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilderness_Medical_Society "Wilderness Medical Society"), the [American Alpine Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Alpine_Club "American Alpine Club"), the [Association of Space Explorers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Space_Explorers "Association of Space Explorers"), the [Experimental Aircraft Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_Aircraft_Association "Experimental Aircraft Association"), and the [Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_Owners_and_Pilots_Association "Aircraft Owners and Pilots Association"). He is president of the board of directors of the [Challenger Center for Space Science Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Challenger_Center_for_Space_Science_Education "Challenger Center for Space Science Education"), and serves on the boards of the [Houston Museum of Natural Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Museum_of_Natural_Science "Houston Museum of Natural Science"), the University of Texas McDonald Observatory and [OceanGate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OceanGate "OceanGate").

In 2014, Parazynski was appointed as a professor of practice at [Arizona State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arizona_State_University "Arizona State University"), and was designated ASU's first University Explorer.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-8) He subsequently founded Fluidity Technologies[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-9) based on his intellectual property, a company aiming to manufacture and distribute novel control devices for mobility in 3-D space, for everything from drones and computer games to VR and surgical robotics.

## Medical career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Medical career")]

While an [undergraduate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduate "Undergraduate") at [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University"), Parazynski studied [antigenic shift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antigenic_shift "Antigenic shift") in [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa")[sleeping sickness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_trypanosomiasis "African trypanosomiasis"), using sophisticated [molecular biology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molecular_biology "Molecular biology") techniques. During [medical school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_school "Medical school"), he was awarded a NASA graduate student [fellowship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scholarship "Scholarship") and conducted [research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research "Research") at [NASA Ames Research Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NASA_Ames_Research_Center "NASA Ames Research Center") on [fluid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fluid "Fluid") shifts that occur during human [space flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_flight "Space flight"). Additionally, he has been involved in the design of several [exercise](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exercise "Exercise") devices that are being developed for long-duration [space flight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_flight "Space flight"), and has conducted research on high-[altitude acclimatization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altitude_acclimatization "Altitude acclimatization"). Parazynski has numerous publications in the field of space [physiology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physiology "Physiology"), and has a particular expertise in human [adaptation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adaptation_(biology) "Adaptation (biology)") to stressful environments.

## NASA career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: NASA career")]

Selected as an astronaut in March 1992, Parazynski reported to the [Johnson Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johnson_Space_Center "Johnson Space Center") in August 1992. He completed one year of training and evaluation, and was qualified as a mission specialist. Parazynski initially served as one of the crew representatives for [extra-vehicular activity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extra-vehicular_activity "Extra-vehicular activity") (EVA) in the Astronaut Office Mission Development Branch. Following his first flight, he was assigned as a backup for the third American long-duration stay aboard Russia's [space station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_station "Space station")[Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mir "Mir"), and was expected to serve as a prime crew member on a subsequent mission. He spent five months in training at the [Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gagarin_Cosmonaut_Training_Center "Gagarin Cosmonaut Training Center"), [Star City, Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_City,_Moscow "Star City, Moscow"), Russia.

In October 1995, when sitting-height parameters raised concerns about his fitting safely in the [Soyuz spacecraft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soyuz_spacecraft "Soyuz spacecraft") in the event of an emergency on board the Mir station, he was deemed too tall for the mission and was withdrawn from Mir training. He has served as the Astronaut Office Operations Planning Branch crew representative for [Space Shuttle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle "Space Shuttle"), Space Station and Soyuz training, and also served as Deputy (Operations and Training) of the Astronaut Office [ISS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") Branch. Most recently, he served as Chief of the Astronaut Office EVA Branch. A veteran of five space flights, [STS-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-66 "STS-66") (1994), [STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86") (1997), [STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95") (1998), [STS-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-100 "STS-100") (2001), and STS-120 (2007), Parazynski has logged over 1,019 hours (8 weeks) in space, including 47 hours of EVA, and traveled over 17 million miles. Parazynski's most recent mission was STS-120, during which he performed four spacewalks to continue International Space Station assembly. The fourth EVA is considered one of the most challenging and dangerous ever performed: while perched on the end of a 90-foot robotic boom, further away from the safety of the airlock than anyone had previously ventured, he had to repair a fully energized solar array. He became only the second NASA astronaut to perform four spacewalks during a single shuttle mission. A photo that he took during one of the spacewalks was listed on _[Popular Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular\_Science "Popular Science")_'s photo gallery of the best [astronaut selfies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astronaut_selfie "Astronaut selfie").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-21)

## Spaceflight experience

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Spaceflight experience")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg/250px-Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Scott_Parazynski_space.jpg)

Scott Parazynski during a spacewalk during STS-120.

The [STS-66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-66 "STS-66") Atmospheric [Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laboratory "Laboratory") for Applications and Science-3 (ATLAS-3) mission was launched from [Kennedy Space Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida"), on November 3, 1994, and returned to land at [Edwards Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwards_Air_Force_Base "Edwards Air Force Base"), [California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California "California"), on November 14, 1994. ATLAS-3 was part of an ongoing program to determine the Earth's [energy balance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_energy_budget#Earth's_energy_imbalance_(EEI) "Earth's energy budget") and [atmospheric](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Earth's_atmosphere "Earth's atmosphere") change over an 11-year [solar cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_cycle "Solar cycle"), particularly with respect to humanity's impact on global-[ozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ozone "Ozone") distribution. Parazynski had responsibility for a number of on-orbit activities including operation of the ATLAS experiments and [Spacelab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacelab "Spacelab") Pallet, as well as several secondary experiments in the crew cabin. He and his crewmates also successfully evaluated the Interlimb Resistance Device, a free-floating exercise he developed to prevent [muscular atrophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muscular_atrophy "Muscular atrophy") in [microgravity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microgravity "Microgravity"). [Space Shuttle _Atlantis_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space_Shuttle_Atlantis "Space Shuttle Atlantis") circled the earth 175 times and traveled over 4.5 million miles during its 262-hour and 34-minute flight.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

[STS-86](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-86 "STS-86")_Atlantis_ (September 25 to October 6, 1997) was the seventh mission to rendezvous and dock with the Russian Space Station Mir. Highlights of the mission included the exchange of U.S. crew members [Michael Foale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Foale "Michael Foale") and [David Wolf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Wolf_(astronaut) "David Wolf (astronaut)"), the transfer of 10,400 pounds of science and logistics, and the first Shuttle-based joint American-Russian spacewalk. Parazynski served as the flight engineer (MS2) during the flight, and was also the navigator during the Mir rendezvous. Parazynski (EV1) and Russian [cosmonaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmonaut "Cosmonaut")[Vladimir Titov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Titov_(cosmonaut) "Vladimir Titov (cosmonaut)") performed a 5-hour, 1 minute [spacewalk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spacewalk "Spacewalk") during which they retrieved four experiment packages first deployed during the [STS-76](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-76 "STS-76")[Shuttle-Mir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuttle-Mir "Shuttle-Mir") docking mission. They also deployed the Spektr Solar Array Cap, which was designed to be used in a future Mir spacewalk to seal a leak in the Spektr module's damaged hull. Other objectives of EVA included the evaluation of common EVA tools to be used by astronauts wearing either Russian or American-made spacesuits, and a systems flight test of the Simplified Aid for EVA Rescue (SAFER). Space Shuttle _Atlantis_ circled the Earth 169 times and traveled over 4.2 million miles during its 259-hour and 21-minute flight, landing at the Kennedy Space Center.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6a/Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg/250px-Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Astronaut_Scott_Parazynski_repairs_a_damaged_ISS_solar_panel.jpg)

 Scott Parazynski during an STS-120 spacewalk to repair a damaged [solar panel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solar_panel "Solar panel") of the [International Space Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station").

[STS-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-95 "STS-95")_[Discovery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Discovery "Space Shuttle Discovery")_ (October 29 to November 7, 1998) was a nine-day mission during which the crew supported a variety of research payloads, including deployment of the Spartan solar-observing spacecraft and the testing of the [Hubble Space Telescope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubble_Space_Telescope "Hubble Space Telescope") Orbital Systems Test Platform. The crew also conducted investigations on the correlation between space flight and the aging process. Parazynski was the flight engineer (MS2) for the mission, as well as the navigator for the Spartan spacecraft rendezvous. During the flight, he also operated the Shuttle's robotic arm in support of the testing of several space-vision systems being considered for ISS assembly. In addition, he was responsible for monitoring several life sciences investigations, including those involving crewmate [Senator John Glenn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Glenn "John Glenn"). The mission was accomplished in 134 Earth orbits, traveling 3.6 million miles in 213 hours and 44 minutes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

[STS-100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/STS-100 "STS-100")_[Endeavour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Space\_Shuttle\_Endeavour "Space Shuttle Endeavour")_ (April 19 to May 1, 2001) was the 9th mission to the International Space Station (ISS) Alpha during which the crew successfully delivered and installed the Space Station "Canadarm2" robotic arm, to be used for all future Space Station assembly and maintenance tasks. Parazynski conducted two spacewalks with [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians "Canadians") colleague [Chris Hadfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hadfield "Chris Hadfield") to assemble and power the next generation robotic arm. Additionally, the pair installed a new [UHF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UHF "UHF")[radio antenna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radio_antenna "Radio antenna") for space-to-space communications during Space Shuttle rendezvous and ISS extravehicular activity. A critical on-orbit spare, a [direct current](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_current "Direct current") switching unit, was also transferred to Alpha during the 14 hours and 50 minutes of EVA work. Also during the flight, Parazynski operated _Endeavour_'s robotic arm to attach, and later detach, the Italian-built _Raffaello_[Multi-Purpose Logistics Module](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-Purpose_Logistics_Module "Multi-Purpose Logistics Module"). Traveling 4.9 million miles in 283 hours and 30 minutes, the mission was accomplished in 186 Earth orbits.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-NASA-22)

STS-120_Discovery_ (October 23 – November 7, 2007) launched from and returned to land at the Kennedy Space Center, Florida. During the mission, the Node 2 module named _Harmony_ was delivered to the International Space Station. This element opened up the capability for future international laboratories to be added to the station. Parazynski served as EV1 (lead spacewalker) and accumulated over 27 EVA hours in 4 spacewalks. One of the major EVA mission objectives was the relocation of the P6 Solar Array from the top of the Z1 Truss to the end of the port side of the Integrated Truss Structure. During the IVA-commanded re-deploy of the solar array, several array panels snagged and were damaged, requiring an unplanned spacewalk to successfully repair the array. The mission was accomplished in 238 Earth orbits, traveling 6.2 million miles in 15 days, 2 hours, and 23 minutes.

## Book

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Scott_E._Parazynski&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Book")]

In 2017, Parazynski's book, _The Sky Below: A True Story of Summits, Space and Speed_,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-23) with co-author Susy Flory, was published. [Homer Hickam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer_Hickam "Homer Hickam") called it “a wonder, a fellow who has packed in more exploits in his lifetime than most of us can imagine.”[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scott_E._Parazynski#cite_note-24)

**Steven Gerald Clifford** (born September 17, 1961) is an American professional [basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basketball "Basketball") coach and executive who serves as a coaching advisor for the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards") of the [National Basketball Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Basketball_Association "National Basketball Association") (NBA). He has previously served as the head coach of the [Charlotte Hornets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Hornets "Charlotte Hornets") and Orlando Magic.

## Early life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Born in [Island Falls, Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_Falls,_Maine "Island Falls, Maine"), Clifford grew up in [Mattawamkeag, Maine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mattawamkeag,_Maine "Mattawamkeag, Maine"), until the third grade, when he moved to [Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vermont "Vermont").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-1) He played varsity basketball under Gerald Clifford, his father and head coach at [North Country Union High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Country_Union_High_School "North Country Union High School") in [Newport, Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_(city),_Vermont "Newport (city), Vermont").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-maine_native-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-3)

Clifford attended the [University of Maine at Farmington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Maine_at_Farmington "University of Maine at Farmington"), where he played [college basketball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_basketball "College basketball") for four years. In his final two seasons, he was team captain and was named Best Defensive Player. He graduated with a degree in [special education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_education "Special education").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-4)

## Coaching career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Coaching career")]

After graduating from college, Clifford became a teacher at [Woodland High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodland_High_School_(Maine) "Woodland High School (Maine)") in Maine. He also gained his first coaching experience at the school, serving as their [head coach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Head_coach "Head coach") for two seasons while leading them to two tournaments.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-maine_native-2)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-nba_profile-5) He then served as an assistant coach at [St. Anselm College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Anselm_College "St. Anselm College"), [Fairfield University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairfield_University "Fairfield University"), [Boston University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_University "Boston University") and [Siena College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siena_College "Siena College"). In 1995, he assumed the head coaching duties at [Adelphi University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adelphi_University "Adelphi University") and coached for four seasons leading his team to four appearances in the NCAA Division II Tournament, an 86–36 (.705) record and four consecutive 20-win seasons. He was the first coach in the school's history with back-to-back 20-plus-win seasons.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-nba_profile-5)

Clifford became an NBA assistant coach with the [New York Knicks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Knicks "New York Knicks") and [Houston Rockets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_Rockets "Houston Rockets") under [Jeff Van Gundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Van_Gundy "Jeff Van Gundy") and quickly developed a reputation as a defensive expert. He then was an assistant for Stan Van Gundy with the Orlando Magic.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-maine_native-2) He considers both the Van Gundy brothers as mentors.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-6) He reached the NBA playoffs in each of his five seasons with Orlando, appearing in the NBA Finals in 2009.

Clifford then joined the [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers "Los Angeles Lakers") in [2012–13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012%E2%80%9313_Los_Angeles_Lakers_season "2012–13 Los Angeles Lakers season") as an assistant.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-7)

### Charlotte Bobcats/Hornets

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Charlotte Bobcats/Hornets")]

On May 29, 2013, Clifford was hired by the [Charlotte Bobcats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Bobcats "Charlotte Bobcats") to be their head coach.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-nba_05292013-8)

Clifford implemented a defensive mentality in Charlotte during his first year as head coach turning the [Charlotte Bobcats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Bobcats "Charlotte Bobcats") into a top five defensive team when in the years prior to his tenure they ranked near the bottom of the NBA in that category. He led the Bobcats to the [2014 NBA playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_NBA_playoffs "2014 NBA playoffs") in his first year as head coach, during which he coached the Bobcats to a 43–39 record. The two years prior to him joining the Bobcats only had a combined total of 28 wins. He was named Eastern Conference Coach of the Month for April 2014 after he led the Bobcats to a 7–1 record leading to the playoffs. He finished fourth in Coach of the Year voting in his first year. On December 6, 2017, it was announced that Clifford would not coach indefinitely to deal with his health issue.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-10) On January 11, 2018, the Hornets announced that Clifford was medically cleared to return to coaching[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-11) after a 21-game absence after dealing with [sleep deprivation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sleep_deprivation "Sleep deprivation").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-12) After the [2017–18 regular season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017%E2%80%9318_NBA_season "2017–18 NBA season"), he was fired as head coach on April 13, 2018, after five seasons coaching the team to a 196–214 record total.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-13)

### Orlando Magic

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Orlando Magic")]

On May 30, 2018, Clifford was named the head coach of the Orlando Magic.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-14)

The Magic started the 2018–19 season by splitting their first 24 games before falling 11 games under .500 after a 126–117 loss to the [Oklahoma City Thunder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oklahoma_City_Thunder "Oklahoma City Thunder").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-15) Despite the dismal start, Clifford led the Magic on a dramatic turnaround. On April 7, 2019, Orlando defeated the [Boston Celtics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Celtics "Boston Celtics") 116–108 to clinch their first playoff berth since the [2011–12 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011%E2%80%9312_Orlando_Magic_season "2011–12 Orlando Magic season").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-16) The win also clinched the Magic's first [Southeast Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Division_(NBA) "Southeast Division (NBA)") title since the [2009–10 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009%E2%80%9310_Orlando_Magic_season "2009–10 Orlando Magic season"). This was the Magic's first playoff appearance since trading [Dwight Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dwight_Howard "Dwight Howard") to the [Los Angeles Lakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Lakers "Los Angeles Lakers") in 2012,[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-17) ending the longest playoff drought in franchise history.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-18)

On June 5, 2021, Clifford and the Magic decided to part ways.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-19)

### Charlotte Hornets (second stint)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Charlotte Hornets (second stint)")]

After the [2021–22 NBA season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021%E2%80%9322_NBA_season "2021–22 NBA season") concluded, the Hornets re-hired Clifford as their head coach on June 24, 2022.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-20)

On April 3, 2024, the Hornets announced that Clifford would step down as head coach at the end of the [2023–24 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023%E2%80%9324_NBA_season "2023–24 NBA season") and move into a front-office advisory role.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-21)

### Phoenix Suns

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Phoenix Suns")]

On August 13, 2025, the [Phoenix Suns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenix_Suns "Phoenix Suns") hired Clifford to serve as a coaching advisor under head coach [Jordan Ott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordan_Ott "Jordan Ott").[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-22)

### Washington Wizards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Steve_Clifford&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Washington Wizards")]

On July 6, 2026, the [Washington Wizards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Wizards "Washington Wizards") hired Clifford to serve as an advisor under head coach [Brian Keefe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Keefe "Brian Keefe").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steve_Clifford#cite_note-23)
